Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning

Yuli Liu Affiliation:  Smart Ocean Technology, University of Macau, Macao SAR, China    Zhiheng Zhang ††thanks: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Corresponding author: Zhiheng Zhang. Email: zhangzhiheng@mail.shufe.edu.cn. Project: https://ylliua1116.github.io/causal-ucb/. Code: https://github.com/ylliua1116/causal-ucb. Affiliation:  School of Statistics and Data Science, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Affiliation:  Institute of Big Data Research, Shanghai University of Finance and EconomicsShanghai 200433, P.R. China
Abstract

Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration’s no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates {ηt}\{\eta_{t}\}, we prove lower bounds of Ω((1+∑tηt)−1/2)\Omega((1+\sum_{t}\eta_{t})^{-1/2}) on minimax inference error and Ω⁡(∑tηt)\Omega(\sum_{t}\eta_{t}) on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of 1.7321.732 versus 6.3266.326 for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of 30.60730.607 and 23.21723.217, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.

1 Introduction

At each slow decision round, a network operator chooses a global configuration, while adaptive, interacting local controllers determine the realized actions and settle into a steady state. The deployment objective is the configuration’s no-exploration steady-state utility, not the reward observed under the measurement policy used to collect data. Exploration can improve action support, but it also changes local actions and post-burn-in contexts. Consequently, a configuration that performs well under exploratory logging need not maximize deployment utility.

Different controllers can generate identical exploratory observations while having different no-exploration steady-state values (Proposition 3). Identifying the target value therefore requires information beyond an accurate outcome model. Evaluation requires an appropriate exposure representation for network interference, correction for target-action mismatch, and a justified link between exploratory and target context distributions. In particular, action overlap supports comparisons conditional on observed contexts, but does not by itself identify the context distribution that would arise without exploration. These requirements must be distinguished when evaluating configurations and making online choices.

Our setting connects causal inference under network interference [1, 2, 3], doubly robust off-policy evaluation and logged-feedback learning [4, 5, 6], and online decision-making with network interference [7, 8, 9, 10]. These research lines provide tools for representing interference, correcting action-law mismatch, and guiding sequential decisions. Our setting differs in both the decision unit and the target: the operator selects a global configuration, while its value is defined after black-box controllers settle under the no-exploration law. The resulting problem is to use exploratory steady-state telemetry for online selection while accounting for the distinct measurement and deployment regimes.

We address this problem with CAUSAL-UCB. An exposure-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator estimates each configuration’s target value, and a predecision certificate separates sampling fluctuation from identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. The certificate is used to select configurations by optimistic target values rather than raw exploratory rewards. The corresponding guarantees rely on the calibration conditions developed in Section 4. This separation makes explicit which uncertainties are estimated from logged data and which require additional assumptions or independent information.

Measurement also has two distinct consequences: it affects the information available for identifying target values and can perturb the state whose utility is being optimized. We formalize this identification–deployment tension through a minimax lower bound for predetermined exploration schedules in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. Separately, we establish a regret guarantee for online selection when the certificates are valid and selected information grows. Under known local interference, we also derive an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared predecision radius for estimation, selection, and reporting.

Contributions. (1) We formalize online causal configuration around the no-exploration steady-state estimand and derive an exposure-aware doubly robust evaluator with a uniform certificate separating sampling fluctuation from identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. (2) For every finite horizon and predetermined exploration schedule in the stated family, we prove minimax lower bounds Ω((1+∑tηt)−1/2)\Omega((1+\sum_{t}\eta_{t})^{-1/2}) for inference error and Ω⁡(∑tηt)\Omega(\sum_{t}\eta_{t}) for measurement-induced deployment loss. We also establish a regret guarantee under valid certificates and selected-information growth. (3) Under known local interference, we establish an anytime finite-sample certificate whose predecision radius is shared by estimation, selection, and reporting.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 formalizes the operational setting and target estimand; Section 4 develops the estimator, certificates, and theoretical guarantees; Section 5 evaluates decision quality, identification–deployment trade-offs, and transfer across network traces. Section 6 concludes. Additional proofs, experimental protocols, and robustness analyses are provided in the appendices.

2 Related Work

\scriptsize1⃝ Causal inference with interference. Potential-outcome methods formalize causal effects under partial or general interference [1, 2, 3]. Causal representation learning further investigates interventional structure, temporal effects, and partial observability [11, 12, 13]. Recent design-based work studies covariate adjustment under approximate neighborhood interference [14], but does not address exploration-induced shifts in the steady-state context law. We explicitly budget exposure and transport error.

\scriptsize2⃝ Off-policy evaluation and overlap.

Doubly robust evaluation, counterfactual risk minimization, and orthogonal nuisance fitting provide complementary tools for learning from logged data [4, 5, 6, 15]. Exponential smoothing [16] and marginal density-ratio estimation [17] address related off-policy evaluation difficulties, while risk–return benchmarking studies downstream policy selection [18]. Overlap-weighted temporal estimation [19] and future-dependent evaluation under partial observability [20] address distinct longitudinal challenges. These methods do not by themselves align exploratory contexts with the no-exploration steady-state law. Action correction and context transport therefore remain separate identification requirements here.

\scriptsize3⃝ Sequential choice and information cost. Optimism-based bandits use uncertainty to guide sequential decisions [21, 22, 23]. Contextual bandit methods examine cumulative versus simple regret [24], heterogeneous multi-agent learning [25], and structured cross-learning [26]. Network-interference bandits and design-based approaches study interacting rewards and inference–regret trade-offs [7, 8, 9, 10]. Variance-dependent and second-order regret analyses provide complementary contextual-bandit guarantees [27, 28]. These lines do not directly address the identification of a global configuration’s no-exploration steady-state value from exploration-perturbed telemetry. Proposition 3 formalizes this identification requirement.

3 Operational Setup and Causal Identification

We formalize deployment logs and an interference-aware action–exposure representation, then define the no-exploration steady-state value as the target of configuration selection. This formulation distinguishes exploratory measurements from deployment objectives and makes explicit the identification requirements underlying subsequent causal evaluation and certification.

3.1 Deployment Logs and the Target Object

We consider a networked system with NN nodes and a compact configuration set 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. At slow round tt, the operator deploys a global configuration zt∈𝒵z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z} and a measurement-level exploration rate ηt∈[0,1]\eta_{t}\in[0,1]. After TburnT_{\mathrm{burn}} fast adaptation steps, the operator records T0T_{0} post-burn-in windows. A logged window contains the realized low-level action Ai,s(t)A_{i,s}^{(t)}, context Ci,s(t)C_{i,s}^{(t)}, and normalized utility Ri,s(t)R_{i,s}^{(t)} for node ii and window ss, with |Ri,s(t)|≤Bu|R_{i,s}^{(t)}|\leq B_{u} after KPI normalization. We write Oi,s(t)=(Ai,s(t),Ci,s(t),Ri,s(t))O_{i,s}^{(t)}=(A_{i,s}^{(t)},C_{i,s}^{(t)},R_{i,s}^{(t)}) for each logged observation, 𝒟t={Oi,s(t):i=1,…,N,s=1,…,T0}\mathcal{D}_{t}=\{O_{i,s}^{(t)}:i=1,\ldots,N,\ s=1,\ldots,T_{0}\} for the batch collected in round tt, and 𝒟≤t=⋃r=1t𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{\leq t}=\bigcup_{r=1}^{t}\mathcal{D}_{r} for the cumulative log.

3.2 Exposure Interface for Network Interference

A direct formulation over the full node-level action profile A1:N,s(t)A_{1:N,s}^{(t)} is statistically and operationally impractical because local controllers are black-box and mutually interfering. We instead use an auditable exposure interface:

Ei,s(t)=ϕi​({Aj,s(t)}j∈𝒩i​(s),Ss(t),Gs(t)),A~i,s(t)=(Ai,s(t),Ei,s(t)).E_{i,s}^{(t)}=\phi_{i}\!\left(\{A_{j,s}^{(t)}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(s)},S_{s}^{(t)},G_{s}^{(t)}\right),\qquad\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(t)}=\bigl(A_{i,s}^{(t)},E_{i,s}^{(t)}\bigr). (1)

Here A~i,s(t)\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(t)} is the joint action/exposure treatment unit. The pre-action context Ci,s−,(t)C_{i,s}^{-,(t)} contains only information available before the focal action is generated; contemporaneous telemetry used by ϕi\phi_{i} belongs to the observed exposure. We score O~i,s(t)=(A~i,s(t),Ci,s−,(t),Ri,s(t))\widetilde{O}_{i,s}^{(t)}=\bigl(\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(t)},C_{i,s}^{-,(t)},R_{i,s}^{(t)}\bigr), while retaining the raw telemetry in 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. The map ϕi\phi_{i} may summarize neighbor load, interference power, top-kk congestion, or graph features [2, 1, 3]; Ss(t)S_{s}^{(t)} and Gs(t)G_{s}^{(t)} denote system telemetry and graph state. Exposure summarizes realized neighboring actions, not an assigned treatment.

Let 𝒜~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}} be the joint action/exposure space. For candidate zz, gz,0​(a~∣c−)g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) is the target law and gz,ηobs​(a~∣c−)g^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) is the law induced by the actual logging mechanism; a round-rr observation uses its source-regime law (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}), fitted as g^b,r\widehat{g}_{b,r}. Because exposure depends on multiple contemporaneous actions, the joint law need not inherit the marginal focal-action mixture. The DR score therefore requires the actual joint action/exposure probability or density, not merely the marginal propensity of AiA_{i}.

Identification requires consistency for this treatment/exposure unit, conditional exchangeability and overlap given C−C^{-}, absolute continuity of the target joint law with respect to the source behavior law, and calibrated response transport across source regimes. These assumptions are not implied by relabeling context. These identification conditions follow standard causal principles [29]. The calibrated budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\exp}(z) accounts for exposure approximation and response-transport discrepancies (Section 4). We audit exposure sufficiency by comparing ϕi\phi_{i} with an enriched map ϕi+\phi_{i}^{+}, using the discrepancy Δ^exp,t​(z)=|W^tϕ+​(z,0)−W^tϕ​(z,0)|\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{exp},t}(z)=\bigl|\widehat{W}_{t}^{\phi^{+}}(z;0)-\widehat{W}_{t}^{\phi}(z;0)\bigr|. A large discrepancy motivates enrichment or a larger calibrated budget; the comparison is a sensitivity diagnostic, not an independently valid certificate.

3.3 Identification-Only Exploration and the No-Exploration Benchmark

The operator ultimately wants the value of a configuration without measurement perturbations. Let νz,η\nu_{z,\eta} be the post-burn-in distribution of pre-action contexts C−C^{-} induced by configuration zz and exploration rate η\eta. Let mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the no-exploration target-regime conditional response for the joint action/exposure unit. The target value is

W∞​(z,0)=𝔼C−∼νz,0​[∫𝒜~mz​(a~,C−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)],z⋆∈arg⁡maxz∈𝒵​W∞​(z,0).W_{\infty}(z;0)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\left[\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right],\qquad z^{\star}\in\arg\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}W_{\infty}(z;0). (2)

For discrete 𝒜~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}, the integral is the corresponding sum. The deployment-facing regret is

RegT=∑t=1T[W∞​(z⋆,0)−W∞​(zt,0)].\mathrm{Reg}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[W_{\infty}(z^{\star};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)\right]. (3)

Its induced joint law is gz,ηobsg^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}, and each historical score uses the behavior law for its actual source regime (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}). This marginal mixture does not determine the joint exposure propensity, and action correction does not transport the exploratory context law to νz,0\nu_{z,0}; see Appendix B.3. Define the steady-state value under exploration by

W∞​(z,η)=𝔼C−∼νz,η​[∫𝒜~mz​(a~,C−)​gz,ηobs​(𝑑a~∣C−)].W_{\infty}(z;\eta)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,\eta}}\left[\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,g^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right]. (4)

The source-regime response discrepancy remains part of the calibrated response-transport budget.

4 Causal Value Certificates and Online Optimization

We develop an exposure-aware clipped doubly robust estimator for the no-exploration steady-state value, together with calibrated deviation certificates. We then characterize the identification–deployment trade-off, analyze optimistic online selection under explicit information-growth conditions, and give an anytime certificate for a restricted known-local-interference model.

4.1 Clipped Doubly Robust Evaluation

Evaluation uses the candidate target joint law g^z,0\widehat{g}_{z,0}, response regression m^z\widehat{m}_{z}, and source-round behavior joint propensity g^b,r\widehat{g}_{b,r}. The target law supplies the direct term and importance numerator; the behavior law supplies the denominator. These nuisance fits are frozen before the corresponding network window is scored, and stored historical scores are never recomputed using later fits. For candidate zz, let

mz​(a~,c−)\displaystyle m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) =𝔼[R∣A~=a~,C−=c−,z,η=0],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[R\mid\widetilde{A}=\widetilde{a},C^{-}=c^{-},z,\eta=0],
μz​(c−)\displaystyle\mu_{z}(c^{-}) =∫𝒜~mz​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(da~∣c−).\displaystyle=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

For an observation from round rr, define the clipped joint importance weight

w^z,r​(a~,c−)=min⁡{g^z,0​(a~∣c−)max⁡{g^b,r​(a~∣c−),πmin},wmax}.\widehat{w}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\min\left\{\frac{\widehat{g}_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}{\max\{\widehat{g}_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),\pi_{\min}\}},w_{\max}\right\}. (5)

The ratio is a probability ratio for discrete treatments and a density ratio (under a common dominating measure) for continuous treatments; πmin\pi_{\min} uses the same convention. The score and pooled estimator are

ψ^z,r​(O~)\displaystyle\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O}) =μ^z​(C−)+w^z,r​(A~,C−)​{R−m^z​(A~,C−)},\displaystyle=\widehat{\mu}_{z}(C^{-})+\widehat{w}_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\}, (6)
μ^z​(C−)\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}_{z}(C^{-}) =∫𝒜~m^z​(a~,C−)​g^z,0​(𝑑a~∣C−),\displaystyle=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\widehat{g}_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-}),
W^t​(z,0)\displaystyle\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0) =1N​T0​t​∑r=1,…,ts=1,…,T0i=1,…,Nψ^z,r​(O~i,s(r)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{NT_{0}t}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r=1,\ldots,t\\ s=1,\ldots,T_{0}\\ i=1,\ldots,N\end{subarray}}\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}\!\left(\widetilde{O}_{i,s}^{(r)}\right). (7)

The inverse-probability component is connected to classical estimation under incomplete observation [30]. Here, the weighting must additionally account for the joint action/exposure treatment law and the distinction between exploratory and target steady-state regimes.

For discrete treatments, the direct-method integrals are sums. The pooled estimator uses 𝒟≤t\mathcal{D}_{\leq t} and is available after round tt for the decision in round t+1t+1. Cross-configuration response differences require the calibrated transport allowance below. With m^z\widehat{m}_{z} clipped to [−Bu,Bu][-B_{u},B_{u}] and weights clipped at wmaxw_{\max}, |ψ^z,r​(O~)|≤Bψ=2​Bu​(1+wmax)|\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})|\leq B_{\psi}=2B_{u}(1+w_{\max}). Appendices B.5–B.7 derive the joint-ratio bounds, DR identity, clipping bias, and nuisance-product expansion [4, 6, 5].

For each candidate zz, nuisance fitting weights past rounds by context similarity rather than pooling them uniformly, using αr,z∝Kh​(d^F​(ν^r,ν^z,0))\alpha_{r,z}\propto K_{h}\!\left(\widehat{d}_{F}(\widehat{\nu}_{r},\widehat{\nu}_{z,0})\right), normalized over r<tr<t. The resulting training-context marginal ν^train,tz\widehat{\nu}^{z}_{\mathrm{train},t} defines the fits for m^z\widehat{m}_{z} and g^z,0\widehat{g}_{z,0}. Weighting addresses context mismatch but does not establish response invariance; a large ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z) triggers local refitting or a wider radius.

4.2 Uniform Causal Value Certificate

The certificate combines fluctuation with calibrated error allowances. For monitoring, let Jt=T0​tJ_{t}=T_{0}t and define the network-window scores as Yj,z=N−1​∑i=1Nψ^z,r⁡(j)​(O~i,j)Y_{j,z}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\psi}_{z,r(j)}(\widetilde{O}_{i,j}), where jj indexes the time-ordered network windows and r⁡(j)r(j) is the deployment round containing window jj. An autocorrelation-based effective sample size is estimated from this aggregated sequence as

n^eff,t​(z)=Jt1+2​∑ℓ=1Ltmax⁡{ρ^ℓ,t​(z),0}.\widehat{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)=\frac{J_{t}}{1+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{t}}\max\{\widehat{\rho}_{\ell,t}(z),0\}}.

The plug-in ESS is diagnostic; n¯eff,t​(z)\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z) must be a calibrated lower-information bound for the aggregated network-window sequence, without assuming within-window node independence. Concentration also requires bounded conditional drift and validated dependence control, such as mixing or block coupling, under the calibration conditions specified in Appendix B.4 and D.1. The adjacent-block diagnostic κ^t​(z)\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z) enters the radius only when calibrated as an upper bound on residual drift.

The calibrated context-shift budget ϵ¯shift,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},t}(z) controls score-averaging transport from the pooled source contexts to νz,0\nu_{z,0}; ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z) controls transfer of bounded context-level nuisance risk from ν^train,tz\widehat{\nu}^{z}_{\mathrm{train},t} to νz,0\nu_{z,0}. Joint-ratio and response-nuisance errors require separate calibration under the actual source-window score laws: context-marginal similarity alone bounds neither joint input-law error nor the no-exploration context law.

The budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) covers exposure-map approximation and cross-configuration/measurement-regime response transport. For the proof, it must dominate the historical average of both target-context response discrepancy and score-level response residual, uniformly over source regimes and prefixes (Appendices B.9, D.3). A narrower exposure-only budget must therefore be expanded and recalibrated. Together with target-joint-law estimation error, nuisance-product error, clipping bias, context transport, and configuration mismatch, the budgets form

ϵ¯tot,t​(z)=\displaystyle\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z)={} ϵm,t​(z)​ϵπ,t​(z)+ϵ¯target,t​(z)+ϵclip,t​(z)\displaystyle\epsilon_{m,t}(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{target},t}(z)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},t}(z) (8)
+ϵexp​(z)+ϵ¯shift,t​(z)+ϵ¯cfg,t​(z).\displaystyle+\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},t}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z).

Here ϵm,t​(z)\epsilon_{m,t}(z) is the response-regression error under source-window score laws, while ϵπ,t​(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z) is the induced clipped joint-ratio error ‖w^z,r−w¯z,r‖L2​(νzr,ηr,gb,r)\|\widehat{w}_{z,r}-\bar{w}_{z,r}\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}},g_{b,r})}, not raw propensity-fit error. The independently calibrated ϵ¯target,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{target},t}(z) bounds first-order error in g^z,0\widehat{g}_{z,0}; calibration details appear in Appendices B.4, B.10, and E.1.

Theorem 1 (Unified deviation certificate).

Fix tt. Assume bounded, predictable/cross-fitted scores; overlap for the joint action/exposure law; a valid exposure/response, shift, and mismatch error budget; and conditional dependence and drift bounds that certify n¯eff,t​(z)\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z) and κ^t​(z)\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z) (Appendices B.4 and D.1). With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously for all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z},

|W^t​(z,0)−W∞​(z,0)|≤2​Bψ​comp⁡(𝒵)+log⁡(2/δ)n¯eff,t​(z)+ϵ¯tot,t​(z)+κ^t​(z).\left|\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0)-W_{\infty}(z;0)\right|\leq 2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})+\log(2/\delta)}{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)}}+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z)+\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z). (9)

Theorem 1 separates sampling error from calibrated nuisance, transport, clipping, and dependence contributions. Diagnostics guide refitting and radius inflation but do not establish coverage; see Appendices B.6–C.1 and C.3.

4.3 The Identification–Deployment Frontier

Exploration affects both the information available for causal evaluation and the utility experienced during deployment. The following lower bound quantifies this identification–deployment tension in a slow-mixing steady-state family.

Theorem 2 (Steady-state identification–deployment frontier).

For each finite horizon TT and predetermined measurement-exploration schedule {ηt}t=1T\{\eta_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, there exists a two-configuration, two-action stationary steady-state family, with potentially horizon-dependent mixing time, such that for any adaptive configuration-selection rule, the minimax expected absolute error of estimating W∞​(z1,0)W_{\infty}(z_{1};0) and the measurement-induced deployment gap satisfy, for universal c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0,

InferenceErrorT≥c11+∑t=1Tηt,DeploymentGapT≥c2​∑t=1Tηt.\mathrm{InferenceError}_{T}\geq\frac{c_{1}}{\sqrt{1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}}},\qquad\mathrm{DeploymentGap}_{T}\geq c_{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}. (10)

Measurement actions reveal latent state through refresh events while also perturbing deployment. The adaptive-data KL and two-point proof is in Appendix D.4; the lower bound characterizes the joint information–deployment problem, not Pareto optimality of CAUSAL-UCB.

4.4 CAUSAL-UCB: Certified Online Optimization

CAUSAL-UCB selects the largest certified upper value after updating nuisance models and diagnostics; the selection schematic is in Appendix E.2.

Theorem 3 (Regret of CAUSAL-UCB).

Assume the confidence event in Theorem 1 holds uniformly over rounds (with roundwise failure-probability allocation), and the selected effective sample sizes satisfy square-root summability. Define et​(z)=ϵ¯tot,t​(z)+κ^t​(z)e_{t}(z)=\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z)+\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z). Then

RegT=O~​(Bψ​T​comp⁡(𝒵)+∑t=2Tet−1​(zt)).\operatorname{Reg}_{T}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(B_{\psi}\sqrt{T\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})}+\sum_{t=2}^{T}e_{t-1}(z_{t})\right). (11)

If et−1​(zt)≤c​t−γe_{t-1}(z_{t})\leq ct^{-\gamma} for 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, the cumulative error is O⁡(T1−γ)O(T^{1-\gamma}). First-round regret is at most 2​Bu2B_{u}. If W∞​(z,η)W_{\infty}(z;\eta) is uniformly LWL_{W}-Lipschitz in η\eta for every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, then the cumulative deployment gap ∑t=1T|W∞​(zt,ηt)−W∞​(zt,0)|\sum_{t=1}^{T}|W_{\infty}(z_{t};\eta_{t})-W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)| is at most LW​∑t=1TηtL_{W}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}.

For finite 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, assume the per-visit condition neff,t−1​(zt)≥λ⁡{1+Nzt​(t−1)}n_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z_{t})\geq\lambda\{1+N_{z_{t}}(t-1)\}. This yields, up to initialization constants,

∑t​eligible1n¯eff,t−1​(zt)≤2​|𝒵|​Tλ,\sum_{t\ \mathrm{eligible}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z_{t})}}\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{Z}|T}{\lambda}},

and hence statistical regret O~​(Bψ​|𝒵|​T​comp⁡(𝒵)/λ)\widetilde{O}(B_{\psi}\sqrt{|\mathcal{Z}|T\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})/\lambda}). For fixed |𝒵||\mathcal{Z}| and λ\lambda, this gives the stated square-root rate; growing |𝒵||\mathcal{Z}| retains the factor |𝒵|/λ\sqrt{|\mathcal{Z}|/\lambda} unless stronger square-root summability is assumed. The information-growth condition is substantive, not implied by optimism; certificate-error and deployment-gap contributions are already stated in Theorem 3. Proofs appear in Appendices D.5, D.6, and C.3.

With known local interference, fixed exploration, homogeneous matched rewards, and known noise scale, the general certificate specializes to a computable anytime radius. In this restricted setting, known neighborhood actions determine whether a logged observation matches the no-exploration target profile. Because the exploration mechanism is fixed and known, the matching probability can be computed directly. We specify the corresponding model and certificate below.

Consider KK configurations and NN nodes. With no-exploration action fixed at zero and exploration action Bernoulli⁡(1/2)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2), local actions are independent Bernoulli⁡(η/2)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta/2) for fixed, known η\eta.

Let each known interference neighborhood contain d=2​r+1d=2r+1 nodes. Define

Ij,i=𝟏​{all actions in node i’s neighborhood equal zero},I_{j,i}=\mathbf{1}\{\text{all actions in node $i$'s neighborhood equal zero}\},

with matching probability q=(1−η/2)d>0q=(1-\eta/2)^{d}>0.

Conditional on Ij,i=1I_{j,i}=1, rewards follow clip⁡(μz+σ​Zj,i,0,1)\operatorname{clip}(\mu_{z}+\sigma Z_{j,i},0,1), with iid Gaussian noise independent of actions and prior deployments and a common law across nodes/windows for each zz. Assume known noise-scale upper bound σ\sigma, wmax≥1/qw_{\max}\geq 1/q, and no hidden interference, context transport, nonstationarity, or burn-in dependence. The target profile is the all-zero neighborhood, logged with probability qq, so the ratio is 1/q1/q on matched windows and zero otherwise; at η=0\eta=0 all nodes are matched, giving the target value Wz=𝔼⁡[clip⁡(μz+σ​Z,0,1)]∈[0,1]W_{z}=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{clip}(\mu_{z}+\sigma Z,0,1)]\in[0,1].

For each configuration zz, index its nn logged network windows by jj. Let Kj=∑i=1NIj,iK_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}I_{j,i}, hj=Kj/(N​q)h_{j}=K_{j}/(Nq), and define the prequential, unclipped, doubly robust score

Yj,z=m^j−​(z)+1N​q​∑i=1NIj,i​(Rj,i−m^j−​(z)),W^z,n=1n​∑j=1nYj,z.Y_{j,z}=\widehat{m}_{j-}(z)+\frac{1}{Nq}\sum_{i=1}^{N}I_{j,i}\bigl(R_{j,i}-\widehat{m}_{j-}(z)\bigr),\qquad\widehat{W}_{z,n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{j,z}. (12)

Here m^j−​(z)\widehat{m}_{j-}(z) is the matched-reward mean available before the deployment round containing window jj (set to 1/21/2 if none exists); all windows in that round use this frozen mean. With M=N​T​T0M=NTT_{0}, define

L\displaystyle L =log⁡2​K​(M+1)δ,\displaystyle=\log\frac{2K(M+1)}{\delta}, (13)
ϵ⁡(m)\displaystyle\epsilon(m) ={1/2,m=0,min⁡{1,σ​2​L/m},m≥1.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1/2,&m=0,\\ \min\{1,\sigma\sqrt{2L/m}\},&m\geq 1.\end{cases} (14)

Let mj−m_{j-} be the matched count available before that deployment round, and mn=∑j=1nKjm_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}K_{j}.

Proposition 1 (Anytime calibrated DR certificate, restricted model).

With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously over every configuration z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and every time at which its data are examined, the projected estimator W~z,n=Π[0,1]​W^z,n\widetilde{W}_{z,n}=\Pi_{[0,1]}\widehat{W}_{z,n} satisfies

|W~z,n−Wz|≤bz,n,bz,n=1n​∑j=1n|1−hj|​ϵ​(mj−)+mnn​N​q​ϵ​(mn).|\widetilde{W}_{z,n}-W_{z}|\leq b_{z,n},\qquad b_{z,n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|1-h_{j}|\epsilon(m_{j-})+\frac{m_{n}}{nNq}\epsilon(m_{n}). (15)

For an as-yet unvisited configuration, use W~z,0=1/2\widetilde{W}_{z,0}=1/2 and bz,0=1/2b_{z,0}=1/2. The certificate can be computed solely from previously logged actions and outcomes. In particular, bz,nb_{z,n} may be used directly for online selection, and its corresponding interval may be reported as the experiment’s confidence interval. It is not a post-hoc interval.

For online selection, let nz​(t−1)n_{z}(t-1) count windows under zz before round tt.

Corollary 1 (Deployment regret conditional on the same certificate).

Choose

zt∈arg⁡maxz∈𝒵​{W~z,nz​(t−1)+bz,nz​(t−1)},z_{t}\in\arg\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\{\widetilde{W}_{z,n_{z}(t-1)}+b_{z,n_{z}(t-1)}\},

with optimism capped at 11 if desired. After at most HH forced initialization rounds, on the simultaneous event of the proposition,

RegT≤H+2​∑t=H+1Tbzt,nzt​(t−1).\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq H+2\sum_{t=H+1}^{T}b_{z_{t},n_{z_{t}}(t-1)}. (16)

Appendix D.7 proves the proposition and corollary using one simultaneous matched-reward event over configurations and examined prefixes, including adaptive decisions. This is the known-mechanism special case of Theorem 1; the general setting instead requires separately calibrated target-law, transport, exposure, and dependence budgets.

Decision implementation.

The experiment initializes each of the five configurations twice (H=10H=10); thereafter it selects the configuration maximizing

min⁡{1,W~z,nz​(t−1)+bz,nz​(t−1)}\min\{1,\widetilde{W}_{z,n_{z}(t-1)}+b_{z,n_{z}(t-1)}\}

and resolves exact upper-bound ties by the current center estimate. The same bb governs selection, reported confidence width, and the corollary’s per-round bound; oracle target values are evaluation-only, while decisions use prior matched observations and predecision radii.

5 Experiments

We evaluate CAUSAL-UCB through four theory-driven questions: \scriptsize1⃝ Certified decisions: Does target-value certification improve online selection under logging–target mismatch? \scriptsize2⃝ Interference and identification: How do exposure, joint overlap, and context shift affect causal evaluation? \scriptsize3⃝ Mechanisms and cost: Which components matter, and how does measurement exploration trade information against deployment utility? \scriptsize4⃝ Trace-driven transfer: Do the findings persist on network-derived traces?

Settings and scope. The controlled benchmark uses a 24-node ring, five configurations, 200 rounds, and 24 paired seeds. METR-LA and FlockLab provide topology and context traces for semi-synthetic replays with model-generated counterfactual outcomes (180 rounds, eight independent seeds per condition); these are not live deployments. A separate 300-seed independent audit assesses full-path certificate coverage (Appendix H.1). We report target regret, final optimality gap, pairwise causal-estimation error, uncertainty width, and deployment gap, distinguishing decision-active certificates from diagnostic widths. Details and robustness checks are in the appendices; empirical performance does not establish the identification assumptions.

5.1 Certified Decision Quality under Mismatch

Protocol. The frozen N=24N=24 ring benchmark uses five configurations, T=200T=200 rounds, T0=2T_{0}=2 retained windows, radius-one interference, exploration rates η∈{0.55,0.08}\eta\in\{0.55,0.08\}, and 24 paired seeds. Oracle target values are evaluation-only.

With clipped-Gaussian noise (σ=0.08\sigma=0.08), we compare certified/legacy DR/IPS, Raw-UCB, Greedy-Raw, and Switchback-OED [31] on five metrics. Only certified widths are decision-active; each of five sensitivity levels uses 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds (Appendix F.3).

Results. Under high mismatch, CAUSAL-UCB attains the lowest regret (1.7321.732), zero terminal gap, and narrowest decision-active width (0.5520.552), versus 6.3266.326 regret and 1.5411.541 width for Certified IPS-UCB. Legacy DR-UCB attains the lowest ATE error (0.0081 versus 0.0230 for CAUSAL-UCB), whereas CAUSAL-UCB achieves substantially lower target regret (1.732 versus 16.647). These results distinguish causal estimation accuracy from online configuration-selection performance. CAUSAL-UCB’s deployment gap (30.60730.607) exceeds Certified IPS-UCB (23.21723.217) and Greedy-Raw (4.1204.120); under low mismatch, Greedy-Raw slightly lowers regret (1.0001.000 vs. 1.0181.018). The separate Pareto analysis is in Appendix F.3.

5.2 Interference, Overlap, and Context Transport

We vary network interference across five levels with 24 paired seeds per condition (Figure 4). Panels (a) and (b) report cumulative target regret and maximum pairwise ATE error, respectively, distinguishing decision quality from causal-estimation accuracy. Since neighboring actions affect realized exposure, focal-action propensity alone cannot characterize the joint action/exposure law. These controlled results assess sensitivity rather than establish identification under arbitrary interference. Oracle values are evaluation-only. We next examine joint-action support and its distinction from post-burn-in context transport.

Conditional action overlap does not determine the no-exploration context law. Figure 5 illustrates context-dependent logging propensities and exploration-induced post-burn-in responses. The paired no-exploration target draws are used for visualization and evaluation only; the policies learn from logged observations. At η=0.55,0.30,0.08\eta=0.55,0.30,0.08, the joint clean-neighborhood probabilities are 0.402,0.623,0.8910.402,0.623,0.891, respectively. The corresponding 10th-percentile match probabilities are 0.250,0.511,0.8480.250,0.511,0.848, and descriptive node-level IPW effective counts are 4,228,7,036,10,2554{,}228,7{,}036,10{,}255.

These diagnostics indicate that action/exposure matching improves as measurement exploration decreases in this controlled setting. However, better joint support does not imply that the exploratory post-burn-in context distribution matches the no-exploration target distribution. Thus, action-law correction and context transport remain separate requirements. The plotted comparisons are sensitivity diagnostics, not independent guarantees of identification or certificate coverage. Additional generator details and support analyses are provided in Appendix G.3.1.

5.3 Mechanisms and the Identification–Deployment Trade-off

Five controlled variants (24 paired seeds, 200 rounds) assess DR correction, exposure, optimism, and exploration.

Removing DR correction or exposure raises regret; omitting exposure yields the largest ATE error (about 0.160.16). No exploration lowers ATE error (about 0.0050.005) but raises regret. The no-OFU ablation changes more than optimism, so it cannot isolate the OFU effect.

The paired optimism study (Appendix G.5) compares Certified-OFU, Certified-Greedy, and Greedy+Decaying-Forced across five initial-information regimes (96 paired seeds each) with shared fits and audits. With an under-sampled optimum, OFU lowers regret from 0.4670.467 to 0.2410.241; across 33 initially misranked seeds, regret is 0.2320.232 versus 1.0771.077 (paired difference 0.8450.845, 95% CI [0.621,1.068][0.621,1.068]). Certified-Greedy wins in the other four regimes.

We next sweep five fixed exploration rates. Regret increases for several baselines but remains relatively stable for Certified DR (Figure 7(a)); this illustrates, rather than proves, Theorem 2. The high-mismatch regret/deployment-gap pairs in panel (b) are (1.732,30.607)(1.732,30.607) for CAUSAL-UCB, (16.207,4.120)(16.207,4.120) for Greedy-Raw, and (6.326,23.217)(6.326,23.217) for Certified IPS-UCB, exposing distinct decision and measurement costs across these methods.

A matched-log 2×22\times 2 DR/IPS-by-exposure study at ρ=1.40\rho=1.40 separately examines estimator and exposure effects (Appendix G.4, Figure 21). Using identical logs across the four conditions separates these effects from differences in data collection.

5.4 Trace-Driven Transfer and Scope

We test transfer on METR-LA [32] and FlockLab [33] topology/context traces with model-generated counterfactual outcomes (180 rounds, eight independent seeds per condition). These are semi-synthetic replays, not live deployments.

Under high mismatch, CAUSAL-UCB reduces regret relative to IPS-UCB on METR-LA (0.7540.754 vs. 0.7740.774) and FlockLab (0.7350.735 vs. 1.6121.612), but has higher deployment gaps than Greedy-Raw. Under low mismatch, Greedy-Raw wins on both traces (2.0102.010 vs. 3.1263.126; 0.7350.735 vs. 5.4725.472), although CAUSAL-UCB attains the lowest FlockLab ATE error (0.00480.0048). The benefits are regime-dependent. Controlled-ring, trace-replay, and 300-seed audit protocols remain separate; eight-seed trace intervals are marginal, not paired. General certificates require calibrated target-action, exposure, context-transport, clipping, and dependence budgets; the anytime result remains restricted to known interference (Appendices D.4, C.3, and C.2).

6 Conclusion

CAUSAL-UCB selects by certified no-exploration steady-state value. We prove a uniform certificate, an identification–deployment lower bound, and regret under calibrated conditions; known local interference yields an anytime radius for estimation, selection, and reporting. Experiments show high-mismatch gains, deployment costs, and low-mismatch reversals across experimental regimes.

Appendix A Problem Origin and Detailed Closest-Work Comparison

The main text establishes the decision primitive: an operator selects a global configuration from post-burn-in exploratory telemetry, but evaluates its no-exploration steady-state value. The identification obstruction and its precise assumptions are developed in Appendix C.2; this section locates the objective relative to the closest research lines.

A.1 Closest-Work Comparison and Scope Boundaries

The main text summarizes the literature by problem dimensions. Here we clarify the closest methodological connections and the distinct estimand and guarantee regimes.

Additional connections arise from heterogeneous causal inference and network geometry. Collaborative causal estimation under heterogeneous data distributions [34] addresses cross-site statistical heterogeneity, whereas geometric analyses of network causal inference [35] study how graph structure can affect the reliability of causal estimation. Neither line directly provides a predecision certificate for the no-exploration steady-state value of a global configuration under measurement-induced regime changes.

Appendix B Extended Setup, Notation, and Estimation Foundations

B.1 Notation and Logged Probability Space

Compact notation table.

Table 5 summarizes the main symbols and experimental settings. Related symbols are grouped by model component; theorem-calibrated quantities and diagnostic-only proxies are distinguished explicitly. The main causal evaluation uses the pre-action context C−C^{-} and the joint action/exposure variable A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E). The original logged tuple OO is distinguished from the derived scoring record O~\widetilde{O}.

Slow and fast time.

The operator chooses a deployment at slow round t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T. Within each round, the system evolves for τ=1,…,Tburn+T0\tau=1,\ldots,T_{\mathrm{burn}}+T_{0}: the first TburnT_{\mathrm{burn}} steps are burn-in, and the final T0T_{0} windows are retained. The raw observation for node ii and retained window ss is

Oi,s(t)=(Ai,s(t),Ci,s(t),Ri,s(t)).O_{i,s}^{(t)}=(A_{i,s}^{(t)},C_{i,s}^{(t)},R_{i,s}^{(t)}).

For causal scoring, the raw log is supplemented with the exposure constructed from the observed network telemetry. We write

Ei,s(t)=ϕi​({Aj,s(t)}j∈𝒩i​(s),Ss(t),Gs(t)),A~i,s(t)=(Ai,s(t),Ei,s(t)),E_{i,s}^{(t)}=\phi_{i}\!\left(\{A_{j,s}^{(t)}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(s)},S_{s}^{(t)},G_{s}^{(t)}\right),\qquad\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(t)}=(A_{i,s}^{(t)},E_{i,s}^{(t)}),

and define the corresponding scoring record as

O~i,s(t)=(A~i,s(t),Ci,s−,(t),Ri,s(t)).\widetilde{O}_{i,s}^{(t)}=\left(\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(t)},C_{i,s}^{-,(t)},R_{i,s}^{(t)}\right).

Here Ci,s−,(t)C_{i,s}^{-,(t)} contains only information available strictly before the focal action is generated. Contemporaneous neighboring actions and telemetry used to construct Ei,s(t)E_{i,s}^{(t)} belong to the observed joint action/exposure variable, not to Ci,s−,(t)C_{i,s}^{-,(t)}. The raw log retains the telemetry needed to construct this scoring record.

Prequential scoring convention.

The main-text notation suppresses the fitting cutoff on the target response regression and target joint law. In the cumulative estimator, ψ^z,r\widehat{\psi}_{z,r} denotes the score rule stored for source round rr: its target-law fit, response-regression fit, and behavior joint-law fit are frozen before the corresponding scoring window is observed. Scores from earlier rounds are retained as stored; they are not retrospectively recomputed using nuisance fits trained on later observations. If nuisance fits are updated within a deployment round, the same convention applies at the network-window level, with a window-specific stored score rule. This is the predictability convention used in the filtration-based concentration arguments.

Latent state and history.

The full state Yτ(t)Y_{\tau}^{(t)} may include queues, controller variables, channel histories, routing tables, or local filters; it and its transition kernel are unknown to the operator. Only logged tuples and runtime diagnostics (e.g., score autocorrelation, block drift, exposure histograms, and context two-sample statistics) are observed. Before round tt, the history is

Ht−1=σ({zr,ηr,Oi,s(r),n¯eff,r,κ^r,ϵ¯shift,r,ϵ¯cfg,r,Δ^exp,r:r<t,i≤N,s≤T0}).H_{t-1}=\sigma\!\left(\left\{z_{r},\eta_{r},O_{i,s}^{(r)},\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},r},\widehat{\kappa}_{r},\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},r},\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},r},\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{exp},r}:r<t,\ i\leq N,\ s\leq T_{0}\right\}\right).

It contains realized deployments and telemetry, not counterfactual observations for configurations that were not deployed. Their values must therefore be evaluated through the exposure interface, the logging law, and the off-policy estimator. In particular, causal evaluation of a candidate configuration requires assumptions that relate the source-regime response to the candidate’s target response; the behavior propensity correction alone does not establish this cross-configuration response relationship.

Target and logging distributions.

Let νz,η\nu_{z,\eta} be the post-burn-in distribution of pre-action contexts C−C^{-} under configuration zz and exploration rate η\eta. Let πz,0​(a∣c−)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-}) denote the target conditional law of the focal local action without measurement exploration, and let ξ⁡(a∣c−)\xi(a\mid c^{-}) be the known exploratory local-action law. The local-action logging mechanism retains its original mixture form:

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)=(1−η)​πz,0​(a∣c−)+η​ξ​(a∣c−).\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})+\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-}).

This equation describes the conditional law of the focal local action. It does not, by itself, imply the same mixture identity for the joint action/exposure variable A~\widetilde{A}, because the exposure may depend on multiple contemporaneous actions and network telemetry.

Write gz,0​(a~∣c−)g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) for the target joint action/exposure law under no-exploration deployment, and gz,ηobs​(a~∣c−)g^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) for the joint law induced by the actual logging mechanism. The latter must be derived from that mechanism; it is not obtained merely by substituting the marginal local-action mixture into a joint propensity. For a historical observation generated in round rr, the behavior joint law corresponds to its actual source regime (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}) and is denoted gb,r​(a~∣c−)g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}). Its fitted version is denoted g^b,r​(a~∣c−)\widehat{g}_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

The target value uses the context law νz,0\nu_{z,0} and the target joint law gz,0g_{z,0}:

W∞​(z,0)=𝔼C−∼νz,0​[∫mz​(a~,C−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)],W_{\infty}(z;0)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\left[\int m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right],

where mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) is the target-regime conditional response under the specified joint action/exposure treatment. The corresponding target conditional mean is

μz​(c−)=∫mz​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−).\mu_{z}(c^{-})=\int m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

For discrete joint treatments, these integrals are sums. For continuous joint treatments, the propensity ratio is interpreted as a density ratio with respect to a common dominating measure.

The target joint law and context law differ from the laws under which historical exploratory observations are collected. The joint importance ratio corrects treatment/exposure-law mismatch only under the corresponding identification, overlap, and response-transport conditions. Context transport from νz,η\nu_{z,\eta} to νz,0\nu_{z,0} and cross-configuration response transport remain distinct requirements; they are not established by the local-action mixture identity alone.
