B.3 Target Value and Logging Law Derivation

The no-exploration target for a candidate configuration zz is

W∞​(z,0)=𝔼C−∼νz,0​[∫𝒜~mz​(a~,C−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)].W_{\infty}(z;0)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\left[\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right]. (17)

Here C−C^{-} denotes the pre-action context, A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E) is the joint action/exposure treatment unit, gz,0(⋅∣C−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid C^{-}) is its target conditional distribution under no-exploration deployment, and mz​(a~,C−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-}) is the corresponding target-regime conditional response mean. For discrete joint treatments, the integral is a sum; for continuous joint treatments, it is taken with respect to the target probability measure.

For deployment under configuration zz and exploration rate η\eta, let νz,η\nu_{z,\eta} denote the post-burn-in distribution of pre-action contexts. The observed focal local action follows the original measurement-level mixture

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)=(1−η)​πz,0​(a∣c−)+η​ξ​(a∣c−).\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})+\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-}).

Consequently,

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)≥η​ξ​(a∣c−).\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})\geq\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-}).

If ξ⁡(a∣c−)≥ξmin>0\xi(a\mid c^{-})\geq\xi_{\min}>0 and η>0\eta>0, the focal-action target-to-logging ratio obeys

πz,0​(a∣c−)πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)≤1η​ξmin.\frac{\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})}{\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})}\leq\frac{1}{\eta\xi_{\min}}.

This is a positivity bound for the marginal focal-action law only. It is not, by itself, a bound on the joint action/exposure importance ratio.

Let gz,ηobs(⋅∣c−)g^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) denote the joint action/exposure law induced by the actual logging mechanism, including the contemporaneous neighboring actions and the exposure mapping. In general, the local-action mixture above does not imply

gz,ηobs​(a~∣c−)=(1−η)​gz,0​(a~∣c−)+η​gξ​(a~∣c−)g^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})+\eta g_{\xi}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})

for any particular joint exploratory law gξg_{\xi} unless that identity is established from the joint action-generation mechanism. In particular, the exposure component may depend on multiple contemporaneous actions and network telemetry, and the joint law must account for those dependencies.

For a historical observation collected in round rr, let (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}) be its actual source regime. Its behavior joint law is the law induced by that source regime, denoted gzr,ηrobsg^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z_{r},\eta_{r}} when the mechanism is known, or gb,rg_{b,r} when represented by the corresponding behavior-law notation. The candidate target law remains gz,0g_{z,0}; these laws need not coincide when zr≠zz_{r}\neq z.

The joint importance ratio used for causal evaluation is

wz,rjoint​(a~,c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−)gb,r​(a~∣c−).w^{\mathrm{joint}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\frac{g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}{g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}.

For continuous joint treatments, this ratio denotes the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the target joint law with respect to the behavior joint law, whenever that derivative exists. A necessary overlap condition is

gz,0(⋅∣c−)≪gb,r(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-})\ll g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-})

for the relevant target contexts and historical source regimes. Any finite upper bound on this joint ratio must be established from the actual joint action/exposure mechanism; it does not follow solely from the marginal mixture formula. The clipped ratio used by the estimator limits the score’s range, while any resulting clipping bias must be included in the calibrated error budget.

Finally, the target context distribution νz,0\nu_{z,0} may differ from the context distribution under which historical observations were collected. Joint action/exposure weighting addresses the treatment-law mismatch conditional on context; it does not, by itself, transport the context distribution or identify a candidate configuration’s response from observations generated under a different configuration. Those discrepancies require the separately stated context-transport and cross-configuration response-transport conditions in the main certificate.

B.4 Post-Burn-in Blocks, Effective Sample Calibration, and Excess Drift

This section defines the post-burn-in network-window score sequence, its plug-in effective sample size, the operational shrinkage proxy, and the excess block-drift diagnostic κ^t\widehat{\kappa}_{t}. The certified lower- information quantity n¯eff,t\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t} requires a separate dependence calibration.

B.4.1 From network windows to the clipped score sequence

For a fixed candidate configuration zz, flatten the retained windows in observation order into j=1,…,Jtj=1,\ldots,J_{t}, where Jt=T0​tJ_{t}=T_{0}t and jj indexes the pair (r,s)(r,s) of deployment round and retained window. Define the network-window score

Yj,z=1N​∑i=1Nψ^z,r⁡(j)​(O~i,s⁡(j)(r⁡(j))),Y¯t​(z)=1Jt​∑j=1JtYj,z.Y_{j,z}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\psi}_{z,r(j)}(\widetilde{O}_{i,s(j)}^{(r(j))}),\qquad\bar{Y}_{t}(z)=\frac{1}{J_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t}}Y_{j,z}.

The score rule stored for source round r⁡(j)r(j) is frozen before the corresponding network window is scored. By the clipped-score bound in Appendix B.7, |Yj,z|≤Bψ|Y_{j,z}|\leq B_{\psi}. The within-window dependence among nodes is unrestricted; the time-series unit for the concentration and autocorrelation calculations is the aggregated network-window score Yj,zY_{j,z}, not the N​JtNJ_{t} node-level records. This convention matches the normalization of W^t​(z,0)\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0) in the main text.

B.4.2 Variance identity for correlated network windows

If the post-burn-in network-window sequence is approximately second-order stationary, define

γℓ​(z)=Cov⁡(Yj,z,Yj+ℓ,z),ρℓ​(z)=γℓ​(z)/γ0​(z).\gamma_{\ell}(z)=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{j,z},Y_{j+\ell,z}),\qquad\rho_{\ell}(z)=\gamma_{\ell}(z)/\gamma_{0}(z).

Then

Var⁡{Y¯t​(z)}\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\{\bar{Y}_{t}(z)\} =1Jt2​∑j=1Jt∑j′=1JtCov⁡(Yj,z,Yj′,z)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{J_{t}^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t}}\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{J_{t}}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{j,z},Y_{j^{\prime},z})
=γ0​(z)Jt​[1+2​∑ℓ=1Jt−1(1−ℓJt)​ρℓ​(z)].\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma_{0}(z)}{J_{t}}\left[1+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{J_{t}-1}\left(1-\frac{\ell}{J_{t}}\right)\rho_{\ell}(z)\right]. (18)

This motivates the plug-in effective sample size

n^eff,t​(z)=Jt1+2​∑ℓ=1Ltmax⁡{ρ^ℓ,t​(z),0}.\widehat{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)=\frac{J_{t}}{1+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{t}}\max\{\widehat{\rho}_{\ell,t}(z),0\}}. (19)

Positive autocorrelations reduce the estimated information. Negative empirical autocorrelations are not used to claim extra precision, because they are often noisy in short sequences.

B.4.3 Operational ESS shrinkage and calibration requirement

The plug-in value n^eff,t​(z)\widehat{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z) is an empirical estimate. Let BtB_{t} be the number of post-burn-in blocks used to estimate autocorrelation. Define the operational shrinkage proxy

n~eff,t​(z)=max⁡{1,n^eff,t​(z)1+cess​log⁡(2​T/δ)/Bt}.\widetilde{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)=\max\!\left\{1,\frac{\widehat{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)}{1+c_{\mathrm{ess}}\sqrt{\log(2T/\delta)/B_{t}}}\right\}. (20)

This shrinkage rule is an operational heuristic, not a finite-sample lower confidence bound. The quantity n¯eff,t​(z)\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z) used in Theorem 1 must instead be supplied by a proved dependence argument or an independently calibrated lower-information bound for the sequence {Yj,z}\{Y_{j,z}\}. Such calibration must establish that the reported quantity does not exceed the information certified by the dependence model or audit. Empirical autocorrelations alone do not establish coverage. If no valid lower-information calibration is available, the general confidence certificate is not certified.

B.4.4 Excess block drift

The autocorrelation correction addresses temporal dependence but not continued drift after burn-in. Partition the network-window sequence into adjacent blocks ℬ1,t,…,ℬGt,t\mathcal{B}_{1,t},\ldots,\mathcal{B}_{G_{t},t} and define

Y¯g,t​(z)=|ℬg,t|−1​∑j∈ℬg,tYj,z.\bar{Y}_{g,t}(z)=|\mathcal{B}_{g,t}|^{-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}_{g,t}}Y_{j,z}.

The excess block-drift statistic is

κ^t​(z)=[max2≤g≤Gt⁡|Y¯g,t​(z)−Y¯g−1,t​(z)|−cB​Bψ​log⁡(2​T​Gt/δ)ming⁡|ℬg,t|]+.\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z)=\left[\max_{2\leq g\leq G_{t}}|\bar{Y}_{g,t}(z)-\bar{Y}_{g-1,t}(z)|-c_{B}B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2TG_{t}/\delta)}{\min_{g}|\mathcal{B}_{g,t}|}}\right]_{+}. (21)

If adjacent block means differ only by concentration-scale noise, κ^t​(z)=0\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z)=0. If they move beyond that scale, the observed excess flags potential residual drift. The statistic is computable from the clipped network-window scores, but it enters a theorem-backed radius only when a dependence or audit argument validates it as an upper bound on residual mean drift at the stated confidence level.

B.5 Mixture Logging Ratio Bounds

This section records the ratio bounds induced by the measurement-level mixture logging mechanism. We distinguish the marginal focal-action ratio from the joint action/exposure ratio, because the former does not, by itself, establish a bound on the latter.

Lemma 1 (Marginal mixture ratio bounds).

Let

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)=(1−η)​πz,0​(a∣c−)+η​ξ​(a∣c−),ξ⁡(a∣c−)≥ξmin>0,\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})+\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-}),\qquad\xi(a\mid c^{-})\geq\xi_{\min}>0,

where 0<η<10<\eta<1. Then the marginal focal-action target-to-logging ratio

wz,η⋆​(a,c−)=πz,0​(a∣c−)πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)w^{\star}_{z,\eta}(a,c^{-})=\frac{\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})}{\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})}

satisfies

wz,η⋆​(a,c−)≤11−ηwhenever ​πz,0​(a∣c−)>0,w^{\star}_{z,\eta}(a,c^{-})\leq\frac{1}{1-\eta}\quad\text{whenever }\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})>0,

and also satisfies the conservative positivity bound

wz,η⋆​(a,c−)≤1η​ξminw^{\star}_{z,\eta}(a,c^{-})\leq\frac{1}{\eta\xi_{\min}}

for all feasible (a,c−)(a,c^{-}).

Proof.

The first bound follows from

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)=(1−η)​πz,0​(a∣c−)+η​ξ​(a∣c−)≥(1−η)​πz,0​(a∣c−).\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})+\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-})\geq(1-\eta)\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-}).

Dividing by the positive denominator gives

wz,η⋆​(a,c−)≤11−ηw^{\star}_{z,\eta}(a,c^{-})\leq\frac{1}{1-\eta}

whenever πz,0​(a∣c−)>0\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})>0. The second bound follows from

πz,ηobs​(a∣c−)≥η​ξ​(a∣c−)≥η​ξmin\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})\geq\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-})\geq\eta\xi_{\min}

and πz,0​(a∣c−)≤1\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-})\leq 1. ∎

Scope of the marginal bounds.

Lemma 1 concerns only the conditional distribution of the focal local action AA given the pre-action context C−C^{-}. Its bounds do not automatically apply to the joint action/exposure variable A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E). In particular, the exposure EE may depend on neighboring actions and contemporaneous network telemetry, so the marginal mixture identity for AA does not by itself imply a corresponding mixture identity for A~\widetilde{A}.

Joint action/exposure ratio.

For candidate configuration zz, let gz,0(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) denote the target joint action/exposure law under no-exploration deployment. Let gb,r(⋅∣c−)g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) denote the behavior joint law associated with the actual source regime (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}) of historical round rr. The joint importance ratio is

wz,rjoint​(a~,c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−)gb,r​(a~∣c−)w^{\mathrm{joint}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\frac{g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}{g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}

when densities with respect to a common dominating measure exist and the denominator is positive on the target support. More generally, the ratio is the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the target joint law with respect to the behavior joint law.

A necessary overlap condition is

gz,0(⋅∣c−)≪gb,r(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-})\ll g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-})

for the relevant target contexts and historical source regimes. This absolute-continuity condition ensures that target events are not assigned zero probability under the corresponding behavior law. It does not, by itself, imply that the joint importance ratio is uniformly bounded.

For clarity, a bound analogous to the first marginal bound would follow under the additional, explicitly verified joint-mixture condition

gb,r(⋅∣c−)=(1−ηr)gz,0(⋅∣c−)+ηrqz,r(⋅∣c−),0≤ηr<1,g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta_{r})g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-})+\eta_{r}q_{z,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-}),\qquad 0\leq\eta_{r}<1,

where qz,rq_{z,r} is a probability law on the same joint action/exposure space. Under this condition,

wz,rjoint​(a~,c−)≤11−ηrw^{\mathrm{joint}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\leq\frac{1}{1-\eta_{r}}

on the target support. However, this bound applies only when the stated joint-mixture identity actually holds. It cannot be inferred solely from the marginal local-action mixture, and it is not automatically valid when the historical source configuration zrz_{r} differs from the candidate configuration zz.

Accordingly, any finite upper bound on the joint ratio must be justified from the actual joint action-generation mechanism, including the induced exposure distribution and any cross-configuration change. If such a bound cannot be established, the analysis must instead retain the appropriate overlap and clipping-bias conditions without claiming the marginal mixture bound for the joint ratio.

Interpretation.

The marginal mixture bounds provide a positivity guarantee for the focal local action. The joint action/exposure formulation used by the main-text doubly robust estimator requires the corresponding joint-law overlap condition and, where a numerical ratio bound is used, its own justification. The cap wmaxw_{\max} bounds the implemented clipped score; it does not establish joint overlap or eliminate clipping bias. Any clipping bias must remain accounted for in ϵclip,t​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},t}(z), as specified in the main certificate.

B.6 Oracle Doubly Robust Identity

Fix a candidate configuration zz. Let C−C^{-} denote the pre-action context and let A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E) denote the joint action/exposure treatment unit. Write gz,0​(a~∣c−)g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) for the target joint law under no-exploration deployment and

μz​(c−)=∫𝒜~mz​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−),\mu_{z}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

where mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) is the target-regime conditional response mean.

For a historical observation collected in round rr, let gb,r​(a~∣c−)g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) denote the behavior joint law associated with its actual source regime. Assume that the target joint law is absolutely continuous with respect to this behavior law on the relevant support. The oracle joint importance ratio is

wz,r​(a~,c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−)gb,r​(a~∣c−).w_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\frac{g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}{g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}.

For continuous joint treatments, this expression denotes the Radon–Nikodym derivative with respect to a common dominating measure.

Let mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the conditional mean of the observed response under the historical source regime. The oracle DR score for candidate zz is

ψz,r​(O~)=μz​(C−)+wz,r​(A~,C−)​{R−mz​(A~,C−)},O~=(A~,C−,R).\psi_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})=\mu_{z}(C^{-})+w_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-m_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\},\qquad\widetilde{O}=(\widetilde{A},C^{-},R).

Conditionally on C−=c−C^{-}=c^{-}, suppose the observed response has conditional mean mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}). Then, whenever the importance ratio is well-defined and the relevant expectations exist,

𝔼b,r​[ψz,r​(O~)∣C−=c−]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{b,r}\left[\psi_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\mid C^{-}=c^{-}\right] =μz​(c−)+∫𝒜~gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−)​[mb,r​(a~,c−)−mz​(a~,c−)].\displaystyle=\mu_{z}(c^{-})+\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})\bigl[m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})-m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\bigr]. (22)

This follows by conditioning on the joint action/exposure variable and using wz,r​gb,r=gz,0w_{z,r}\,g_{b,r}=g_{z,0} on the target support.

In particular, if the conditional response is invariant between the historical source regime and the target regime on the relevant support, so that

mb,r​(a~,c−)=mz​(a~,c−),m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}),

then the response-discrepancy term in Eq. (22) vanishes and

𝔼b,r​[ψz,r​(O~)∣C−=c−]=μz​(c−).\mathbb{E}_{b,r}\left[\psi_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\mid C^{-}=c^{-}\right]=\mu_{z}(c^{-}).

Averaging this conditional identity over the target context law νz,0\nu_{z,0} gives

𝔼C−∼νz,0​𝔼b,r​[ψz,r​(O~)∣C−]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\mathbb{E}_{b,r}\left[\psi_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\mid C^{-}\right] =𝔼C−∼νz,0​[μz​(C−)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}[\mu_{z}(C^{-})]
=W∞​(z,0).\displaystyle=W_{\infty}(z;0). (23)

The conditional identity and its target-context average require distinct qualifications when historical observations come from other configurations or exploration regimes. If the conditional response differs across source and target regimes, the integral in Eq. (22) is a response-transport discrepancy and must be bounded by the separately calibrated response-transport budget. If the historical context law differs from νz,0\nu_{z,0}, averaging under the historical context law instead of the target context law introduces an additional context-transport discrepancy. Neither discrepancy is removed merely by correcting the joint action/exposure distribution.

Consequently, the oracle identity establishes the DR correction under the stated joint-treatment overlap and response conditions; it does not, by itself, identify the counterfactual response of an unobserved configuration. The plug-in estimator inherits the corresponding target-joint-law estimation, nuisance-product, clipping, exposure/response-transport, context-shift, and cross-configuration mismatch terms, as accounted for in the main-text certificate and the following appendices.

B.7 Clipping Bias and Boundedness

Fix a candidate configuration zz and a historical source round rr. Let C−C^{-} denote the pre-action context and let A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E) denote the joint action/exposure treatment unit. Write gz,0(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) for the target joint law and gb,r(⋅∣c−)g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) for the behavior joint law associated with the actual source regime in round rr.

Assume the target joint law is absolutely continuous with respect to the behavior joint law on the relevant support. Define the oracle joint importance ratio and its clipped version by

wz,r​(a~,c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−)gb,r​(a~∣c−),w¯z,r​(a~,c−)=min⁡{wz,r​(a~,c−),wmax}.w_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\frac{g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})}{g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})},\qquad\bar{w}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=\min\{w_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}),w_{\max}\}.

For continuous joint treatments, the ratio is understood as the Radon–Nikodym derivative with respect to a common dominating measure. The ratio is defined on the behavior support; values outside that support require the stated overlap condition.

Boundedness of the clipped score.

Suppose the normalized response and the fitted response regression satisfy

|R|≤Bu,|m^z​(a~,c−)|≤Bu.|R|\leq B_{u},\qquad|\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})|\leq B_{u}.

Suppose also that the fitted target joint law is a probability distribution and that

μ^z​(c−)=∫𝒜~m^z​(a~,c−)​g^z,0​(𝑑a~∣c−),\widehat{\mu}_{z}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,\widehat{g}_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

so that |μ^z​(c−)|≤Bu|\widehat{\mu}_{z}(c^{-})|\leq B_{u}. The fitted clipped weight satisfies 0≤w^z,r≤wmax0\leq\widehat{w}_{z,r}\leq w_{\max}. Therefore, for the joint-treatment DR score

ψ^z,r​(O~)=μ^z​(C−)+w^z,r​(A~,C−)​{R−m^z​(A~,C−)},\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})=\widehat{\mu}_{z}(C^{-})+\widehat{w}_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\},

where O~=(A~,C−,R)\widetilde{O}=(\widetilde{A},C^{-},R), we have

|ψ^z,r​(O~)|\displaystyle|\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})| ≤Bu+wmax​(|R|+|m^z​(A~,C−)|)\displaystyle\leq B_{u}+w_{\max}\bigl(|R|+|\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})|\bigr)
≤Bu​(1+2​wmax)≤2​Bu​(1+wmax)=:Bψ.\displaystyle\leq B_{u}(1+2w_{\max})\leq 2B_{u}(1+w_{\max})=:B_{\psi}. (24)

Thus the score bound used in the main-text concentration argument remains valid after replacing the marginal action weight by the clipped joint action/exposure weight. The same bound applies to the oracle score when its response regression and target mean satisfy the corresponding boundedness conditions.

Clipping bias.

Let mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the target-regime conditional response, with |mz|≤Bu|m_{z}|\leq B_{u}. Define the oracle unclipped and clipped scores, respectively, by

ψz,ror​(O~)\displaystyle\psi^{\mathrm{or}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O}) =μz​(C−)+wz,r​(A~,C−)​{R−mz​(A~,C−)},\displaystyle=\mu_{z}(C^{-})+w_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-m_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\},
ψz,rclip​(O~)\displaystyle\psi^{\mathrm{clip}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O}) =μz​(C−)+w¯z,r​(A~,C−)​{R−mz​(A~,C−)},\displaystyle=\mu_{z}(C^{-})+\bar{w}_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-m_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\},

where

μz​(c−)=∫𝒜~mz​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−).\mu_{z}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

Because |R−mz​(A~,C−)|≤2​Bu|R-m_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})|\leq 2B_{u}, their pointwise difference obeys

|ψz,ror​(O~)−ψz,rclip​(O~)|≤2​Bu​(wz,r​(A~,C−)−wmax)+,\left|\psi^{\mathrm{or}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})-\psi^{\mathrm{clip}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\right|\leq 2B_{u}\bigl(w_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})-w_{\max}\bigr)_{+},

where (x)+=max⁡{x,0}(x)_{+}=\max\{x,0\}. Consequently, under any common context law ν\nu for which the relevant expectations exist,

𝔼C−∼νA~∼gb,r(⋅∣C−)​[|ψz,ror​(O~)−ψz,rclip​(O~)|]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}C^{-}\sim\nu\\ \widetilde{A}\sim g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid C^{-})\end{subarray}}\left[\left|\psi^{\mathrm{or}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})-\psi^{\mathrm{clip}}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\right|\right]
≤2​Bu​𝔼C−∼νA~∼gb,r(⋅∣C−)​[(wz,r​(A~,C−)−wmax)+].\displaystyle\qquad\leq 2B_{u}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}C^{-}\sim\nu\\ \widetilde{A}\sim g_{b,r}(\cdot\mid C^{-})\end{subarray}}\left[\bigl(w_{z,r}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})-w_{\max}\bigr)_{+}\right]. (25)

The right-hand side is the clipping-bias allowance for this source regime and context law. When multiple historical rounds are pooled, the calibrated allowance must cover their corresponding averaged contributions; a bound for one round alone does not automatically bound the entire historical average.

Role in the causal value certificate.

The clipping allowance ϵclip,t​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},t}(z) must bound the historical-average truncation bias for the joint ratios used by the estimator. It neither establishes overlap when target-supported events are impossible under the behavior law nor covers source-to-target response transport. Likewise, fitted-ratio error is not included in the oracle clipping bound (25); it belongs to the nuisance decomposition in Appendix B.8. The certificate must therefore retain separate calibrated allowances for target-law estimation, nuisance error, context transport, exposure approximation, and response transport.

B.8 Plug-in Nuisance Error: Exact Decomposition and Response Transport

Condition on the nuisance fits stored before a scoring window and on a common evaluation context law ν\nu for the pre-action context C−C^{-}. Fix a candidate configuration zz and a historical source round rr. For compactness, write

p⁡(a~∣c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−),b⁡(a~∣c−)=gb,r​(a~∣c−),p(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})=g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),\qquad b(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})=g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

for the target and behavior joint action/exposure laws. Let mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) be the target-regime conditional response mean and mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) the conditional response mean under the historical source regime.

The fitted quantities below are the versions used by the stored score ψ^z,r\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}; their fitting-cutoff indices are suppressed only for readability. Let p^\widehat{p}, b^\widehat{b}, and m^z\widehat{m}_{z} denote the fitted target joint law, behavior joint law, and target response regression. Define

μ^z​(c−)=∫𝒜~m^z​(a~,c−)​p^​(𝑑a~∣c−),\widehat{\mu}_{z}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\widehat{p}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

and suppose the fitted joint laws are valid probability distributions. For continuous joint treatments, all ratios are density ratios with respect to a common dominating measure, and denominator regularization must be defined consistently with that measure.

Write

w=pb,w¯=min⁡{w,wmax},w^=min⁡{p^max⁡{b^,πmin},wmax},w=\frac{p}{b},\qquad\bar{w}=\min\{w,w_{\max}\},\qquad\widehat{w}=\min\left\{\frac{\widehat{p}}{\max\{\widehat{b},\pi_{\min}\}},w_{\max}\right\},

where ratios are evaluated at (a~,c−)(\widetilde{a},c^{-}). Define

δm=m^z−mz,δw=w^−w¯,Δb,r,z=mb,r−mz.\delta_{m}=\widehat{m}_{z}-m_{z},\qquad\delta_{w}=\widehat{w}-\bar{w},\qquad\Delta_{b,r,z}=m_{b,r}-m_{z}.

Thus δw\delta_{w} is the error in the *induced clipped joint importance ratio*, not merely the raw behavior-density estimation error.

The fitted joint-treatment DR score is

ψ^z,r​(O~)=μ^z​(C−)+w^​(A~,C−)​{R−m^z​(A~,C−)},O~=(A~,C−,R).\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})=\widehat{\mu}_{z}(C^{-})+\widehat{w}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\{R-\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})\},\qquad\widetilde{O}=(\widetilde{A},C^{-},R).

Conditionally on C−=c−C^{-}=c^{-}, the observed response has mean mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) under the behavior law. The exact identity is

𝔼b,r​[ψ^z,r​(O~)∣C−=c−]−∫𝒜~p⁡(a~∣c−)​mz​(a~,c−)​𝑑a~\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{b,r}[\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O})\mid C^{-}=c^{-}]-\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}p(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
=\displaystyle={} ∫𝒜~[p^−p]​(a~∣c−)​m^z​(a~,c−)​𝑑a~\displaystyle\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}[\widehat{p}-p](\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})\widehat{m}_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
+∫𝒜~[p−bw¯](a~∣c−)δm(a~,c−)da~\displaystyle+\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}[p-b\bar{w}](\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})\delta_{m}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
−∫𝒜~b(a~∣c−)δw(a~,c−)δm(a~,c−)da~\displaystyle-\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}b(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})\delta_{w}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\delta_{m}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
+∫𝒜~b(a~∣c−)w^(a~,c−)Δb,r,z(a~,c−)da~.\displaystyle+\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}b(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})\widehat{w}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\Delta_{b,r,z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}. (26)

For discrete joint treatments, the integrals above are sums. The first three terms are the target-joint-law, clipping, and nuisance-product contributions. The fourth term is a separate source-to-target response-transport contribution; it vanishes only under a justified conditional response-invariance assumption. Correcting the joint action/exposure distribution alone does not remove this fourth term.

Bounds for the nuisance terms.

Suppose

|R|≤Bu,|mz|≤Bu,|m^z|≤Bu,|mb,r|≤Bu.|R|\leq B_{u},\qquad|m_{z}|\leq B_{u},\qquad|\widehat{m}_{z}|\leq B_{u},\qquad|m_{b,r}|\leq B_{u}.

For the chosen context law ν\nu, define

𝔼ν,b[f]=𝔼C−∼ν𝔼A~∼b(⋅∣C−)[f(A~,C−)],∥f∥L2​(ν,b)=(𝔼ν,b[f2])1/2.\mathbb{E}_{\nu,b}[f]=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu}\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{A}\sim b(\cdot\mid C^{-})}[f(\widetilde{A},C^{-})],\qquad\|f\|_{L_{2}(\nu,b)}=\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu,b}[f^{2}]\right)^{1/2}.

The first term is bounded by the first-order target-joint-law error

ϵtarget=Bu𝔼C−∼ν[∥p^(⋅∣C−)−p(⋅∣C−)∥1].\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}}=B_{u}\,\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu}\left[\|\widehat{p}(\cdot\mid C^{-})-p(\cdot\mid C^{-})\|_{1}\right]. (27)

Since

p−b​w¯=b​(w−wmax)+,(x)+=max⁡{x,0},p-b\bar{w}=b(w-w_{\max})_{+},\qquad(x)_{+}=\max\{x,0\},

the second term is bounded by

ϵclip,r=2​Bu​𝔼ν,b​[(w−wmax)+].\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},r}=2B_{u}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu,b}[(w-w_{\max})_{+}]. (28)

Here |δm|≤2​Bu|\delta_{m}|\leq 2B_{u} has been used.

By Cauchy–Schwarz, the third term is bounded by

ϵm​π,r=‖δm‖L2​(ν,b)​‖δw‖L2​(ν,b).\epsilon_{m\pi,r}=\|\delta_{m}\|_{L_{2}(\nu,b)}\|\delta_{w}\|_{L_{2}(\nu,b)}. (29)

Accordingly, the main-text ϵm,t​(z)\epsilon_{m,t}(z) and ϵπ,t​(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z) must control these two norms under the actual source-window score laws. A sufficient pooled-prefix convention is to use uniform upper bounds over all source rounds and windows included in the prefix; alternatively, a directly calibrated historical average of the products may be used. A bound on the raw behavior law alone is not sufficient unless it is shown to imply the required bound on ‖w^−w¯‖L2​(ν,b)\|\widehat{w}-\bar{w}\|_{L_{2}(\nu,b)}.

Source-to-target response transport.

The fourth term in Eq. (26) is bounded by

ϵresp,r​(z)\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{resp},r}(z) =𝔼C−∼ν𝔼A~∼b(⋅∣C−)[w^(A~,C−)|Δb,r,z(A~,C−)|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu}\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{A}\sim b(\cdot\mid C^{-})}\left[\widehat{w}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})|\Delta_{b,r,z}(\widetilde{A},C^{-})|\right]
≤wmax​𝔼ν,b​[|Δb,r,z|].\displaystyle\leq w_{\max}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu,b}[|\Delta_{b,r,z}|]. (30)

This bound controls the response-transport term when the score is compared directly with the target conditional mean. In the five-term proof telescope, where the third term is compared with the oracle source-response functional Vz,rlogV_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}, the corresponding score-level residual is instead the signed integral involving (b​w^−p)​Δb,r,z(b\widehat{w}-p)\Delta_{b,r,z}; it is defined and bounded in Appendix D.3. The two expressions serve different decompositions and must not be substituted for one another without the associated algebra.

If the main-text exposure/response budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) is calibrated to dominate the required source-response terms for all admissible historical source regimes and all prefixes, those terms are included there. Otherwise, an additional explicit response-transport allowance is required in the theorem’s error budget. Such an allowance must not be silently omitted or counted twice.

Implications for the certificate.

After pooling, target-law, clipping, nuisance-product, and source-response contributions must be calibrated under the same source regimes, target support, and historical averaging scheme; a one-round bound is insufficient. Target-law error remains first order, and neither cross-fitting nor estimating the marginal local-action mixture identifies the joint action/exposure law or an undeployed configuration’s response.

B.9 Exposure Approximation and Enrichment Diagnostic

Let LL denote the full interference state, which may contain network information not fully captured by the observed exposure mapping. Let C−C^{-} denote the context available strictly before the focal action, and let A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E) denote the observed joint action/exposure treatment unit, where EE is constructed from the available network telemetry.

Under any single fixed probability law, the tower property gives

𝔼[𝔼[R∣L,z]]=𝔼[R∣z]=𝔼[𝔼[R∣A~,C−,z]].\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[R\mid L,z]]=\mathbb{E}[R\mid z]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[R\mid\widetilde{A},C^{-},z]].

Consequently, the difference between these unconditional means under the same law cannot, by itself, quantify exposure approximation error. Such error concerns whether the observed context and exposure representation is sufficient for the conditional response and transport arguments required by the causal estimand, rather than a difference between two representations of the same unconditional expectation.

Let Pz,0P_{z,0} denote the target-regime law under configuration zz without measurement exploration. Write νz,0\nu_{z,0} for its pre-action context law and gz,0(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) for its conditional joint action/exposure law. When the target interventional response is identified on this representation, denote it by mz0​(a~,c−)m_{z}^{0}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}). Thus,

W∞​(z,0)=𝔼C−∼νz,0​[∫𝒜~mz0​(a~,C−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)].W_{\infty}(z;0)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\left[\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}^{0}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right].

This representation requires the corresponding causal identification assumptions under interference; it is not implied merely by defining an observed exposure mapping. If the response mzm_{z} used in the main-text score is not equal to this identified target response, the resulting representation discrepancy must be included in the exposure/response budget.

For a historical observation collected in source round rr, let mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the conditional response under that historical source regime, evaluated at the target context and joint action/exposure arguments. This notation presumes that the source response is meaningful on the relevant target support; the assumptions or error bounds needed to justify that transport must be stated separately. Define the target-joint-law average of the source response by

Vz,rlog​(c−)=∫𝒜~mb,r​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−).V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

The source index rr is retained because the response mechanism may vary with the deployed configuration and exploration regime.

The target-context source-response discrepancy is

ϵexp,rtarget​(z)=|W∞​(z,0)−𝔼C−∼νz,0​Vz,rlog​(C−)|.\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r}^{\mathrm{target}}(z)=\left|W_{\infty}(z;0)-\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})\right|. (31)

If the target response is identified as above and the relevant integrals exist, then

ϵexp,rtarget​(z)\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r}^{\mathrm{target}}(z) =|𝔼C−∼νz,0​∫𝒜~[mz0​(a~,C−)−mb,r​(a~,C−)]​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}[m_{z}^{0}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})-m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})]g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\right|
≤𝔼C−∼νz,0​∫𝒜~|mz0​(a~,C−)−mb,r​(a~,C−)|​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}|m_{z}^{0}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})-m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})|g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-}). (32)

This is a sufficient bound for the response discrepancy under the target context and target joint action/exposure laws. It may be zero under a justified conditional response-invariance assumption, but that invariance does not follow from importance weighting alone.

Scope of the main-text exposure/response budget.

The quantity in Eq. (31) is only the target-context component of the transport argument. In the proof of Theorem 1, the third telescope term also contains the score-level response residual defined in Eq. (62) of Appendix D.3. Therefore the single main-text budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) must be calibrated to dominate the exposure-representation discrepancy, the historical average of the score-level response residuals, and the historical average of the terms ϵexp,rtarget​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r}^{\mathrm{target}}(z), uniformly over the admissible source regimes and prefixes used by the algorithm. Equivalently, one may directly calibrate a tighter bound on the combined response/exposure contribution in the exact telescope. A bound for Eq. (31) alone is not sufficient unless the score-level residual is separately shown to vanish or is otherwise covered.

The component terms are used to define one calibrated envelope ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) in the main theorem; they are not added again as separate terms in ϵ¯tot,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z). This avoids counting the same response-transport contribution twice. If no single envelope has been calibrated for the actual scoring mechanism, the current theorem’s stated error budget is not yet certified for that implementation.

Exposure enrichment as a sensitivity diagnostic.

Let ϕ\phi denote the baseline exposure mapping and let ϕ+\phi^{+} denote an enriched mapping using additional observed network information. The associated change in the fitted value estimate, Δ^exp,t​(z)\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{exp},t}(z), can be used to assess sensitivity to the chosen exposure representation. However, a small change between two fitted regressors is not a certified upper bound on exposure approximation error: both regressors may omit the same latent component of LL.

Accordingly, the exposure/response transport term in Theorem 1 is a valid error allowance only when its calibration covers the relevant representation and source-to-target response discrepancies over the historical windows used by the estimator. The enrichment diagnostic provides supporting sensitivity evidence, not an independent high-probability guarantee. Context -distribution shift and nuisance-training mismatch remain separate terms unless the calibration explicitly covers them.

B.10 Context Shift and Cross-Configuration Mismatch

This section distinguishes context-distribution shift in score averaging from context-marginal mismatch in nuisance training. Neither term is a substitute for the joint action/exposure overlap condition or for the source-to-target conditional response discrepancy defined in Appendix B.9.

Context-shift discrepancy.

Fix a candidate configuration zz and a historical source round rr, whose deployed configuration and exploration rate are (zr,ηr)(z_{r},\eta_{r}). Let νz,0\nu_{z,0} denote the target pre-action context law and let νzr,ηr\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}} denote the source pre-action context law. Define

Vz,rlog​(c−)=∫𝒜~mb,r​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−),V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

where mb,rm_{b,r} is the conditional response under the historical source regime and gz,0g_{z,0} is the target joint action/exposure law. This expression presumes that the source response is meaningful on the relevant target support and that the required integrals exist.

The context-shift discrepancy for this source round is

ϵshift,r​(z)=|𝔼C−∼νzr,ηr​Vz,rlog​(C−)−𝔼C−∼νz,0​Vz,rlog​(C−)|.\epsilon_{\mathrm{shift},r}(z)=\left|\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}}}V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})-\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})\right|. (33)

It compares the same source-response functional under two context laws, so it isolates context-distribution shift from conditional response transport. Combining this definition with Eq. (31), the triangle inequality gives

|W∞​(z,0)−𝔼C−∼νzr,ηr​Vz,rlog​(C−)|≤ϵexp,rtarget​(z)+ϵshift,r​(z).\displaystyle\left|W_{\infty}(z;0)-\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}}}V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})\right|\leq\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r}^{\mathrm{target}}(z)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{shift},r}(z). (34)
Distributional calibration of context shift.

Let dℱd_{\mathcal{F}} be a context-distribution discrepancy, such as a suitably normalized integral probability metric. If a validated calibration map KhK_{h} satisfies

|𝔼ν​h​(C−)−𝔼ν′​h​(C−)|≤Kh​(dℱ​(ν,ν′))\left|\mathbb{E}_{\nu}h(C^{-})-\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\prime}}h(C^{-})\right|\leq K_{h}\!\left(d_{\mathcal{F}}(\nu,\nu^{\prime})\right)

for the relevant function h=Vz,rlogh=V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{log}}, then

ϵshift,r​(z)≤Kh​(dℱ​(νzr,ηr,νz,0)).\epsilon_{\mathrm{shift},r}(z)\leq K_{h}\!\left(d_{\mathcal{F}}(\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}},\nu_{z,0})\right). (35)

The calibration map and its conditions must be justified for the relevant function class. An empirical two-sample statistic alone does not establish this high-probability bound, and an observed context discrepancy does not identify an otherwise unobserved target context law.

For the historical data available before round tt, define

ϵ¯shift,t−1​(z)=1t−1​∑r=1t−1ϵshift,r​(z),\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},t-1}(z)=\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_{r=1}^{t-1}\epsilon_{\mathrm{shift},r}(z), (36)

when the same source context law applies to all T0T_{0} retained windows within each deployment round. If the relevant conditional laws vary across retained windows, the allowance must instead be averaged over those windows with the same normalization as the historical estimator. The bound used by the certificate must cover the actual historical average, not just a single source round.

Cross-configuration nuisance-training context mismatch.

The main text assigns past rounds weights based on their context-law discrepancy from the target context law. Let νz,ttr\nu_{z,t}^{\mathrm{tr}} denote the population context marginal of that weighted training sample, and let νz,0\nu_{z,0} be the target context law. Let ℋcfg\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{cfg}} be the class of bounded context-level conditional score or nuisance-risk functions for which transfer is calibrated, normalized so that |h⁡(c−)|≤Bψ|h(c^{-})|\leq B_{\psi}. Define

ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)=suph∈ℋcfg|𝔼C−∼νz,ttr​h​(C−)−𝔼C−∼νz,0​h​(C−)|.\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z)=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{cfg}}}\left|\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,t}^{\mathrm{tr}}}h(C^{-})-\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}h(C^{-})\right|. (37)

If a validated calibration map KcfgK_{\mathrm{cfg}} controls this function class, then

ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)≤Kcfg​(dℱ​(νz,ttr,νz,0)).\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z)\leq K_{\mathrm{cfg}}\!\left(d_{\mathcal{F}}(\nu_{z,t}^{\mathrm{tr}},\nu_{z,0})\right). (38)

The context-discrepancy weighting in the main text is an operational way to construct νz,ttr\nu_{z,t}^{\mathrm{tr}}; the empirical discrepancy itself is not a high-probability calibration unless the relevant function-class bound is justified.

This ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z) is a context-marginal nuisance- transfer allowance, matching the main-text definition and the finite- state context-audit construction in Appendix C.2. It does not, by itself, bound a mismatch between joint action/exposure input laws or between conditional response functions. Therefore, ϵm,t​(z)\epsilon_{m,t}(z) and ϵπ,t​(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z) must be calibrated under the actual source-window score measures used in Appendix B.8, or their transfer from the fitting measure must be justified separately. In particular, a raw behavior propensity error alone is not a substitute for a bound on the induced clipped joint-ratio error.

Avoiding omissions and double counting.

The context-shift term controls the change in expectation of the source-response functional between the source and target context laws. The configuration term controls only the calibrated context-marginal transfer of nuisance-risk functions. The exposure/response budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) controls the response/exposure contributions specified in Appendix B.9 and the exact proof in Appendix D.3. A source-to-target conditional response discrepancy must not be counted again as a configuration mismatch if it is already included in ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z). Conversely, an input-law or nuisance error not covered by the direct nuisance bounds cannot be silently omitted just because the context marginals are close.

The quantities above are population discrepancies or calibrated upper bounds, not automatic consequences of observed telemetry. Empirical context distances, exposure-enrichment comparisons, and fitted-model diagnostics support sensitivity analysis but do not independently establish the required transport or coverage guarantees.

B.11 Configuration-Aware Nuisance Fitting

Fix a candidate configuration zz and a predecision round tt. The nuisance functions used to evaluate zz target the no-exploration causal estimand, although their fitting sample may contain historical observations collected under other source configurations. This section distinguishes target nuisance functions, the weighted training-context law, and the assumptions required to transport historical response information to the target configuration.

Target nuisance functions.

Let C−C^{-} denote the pre-action context and A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E) the joint action/exposure treatment unit. Write gz,0(⋅∣c−)g_{z,0}(\cdot\mid c^{-}) for the target joint law under configuration zz without measurement exploration. Let mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) be the target-regime conditional response mean and define

μz​(c−)=∫𝒜~mz​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−),W∞​(z,0)=𝔼C−∼νz,0​[μz​(C−)].\mu_{z}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),\qquad W_{\infty}(z;0)=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}[\mu_{z}(C^{-})].

The fitted response regression and target joint law induce

μ^z,r​(c−)=∫𝒜~m^z,r​(a~,c−)​g^z,0,r​(𝑑a~∣c−).\widehat{\mu}_{z,r}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\widehat{m}_{z,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})\widehat{g}_{z,0,r}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

Here the subscript rr records the fitting cutoff used for the score stored for round rr; the main text suppresses this cutoff inside ψ^z,r\widehat{\psi}_{z,r} for readability. The fitted joint law must be a valid probability distribution. For continuous joint treatments, all ratios and integrals use a common dominating measure.

Historical training observations and context weighting.

Let zrz_{r} and ηr\eta_{r} denote the deployed configuration and exploration rate in historical round rr. The scoring record is

O~i,s(r)=(A~i,s(r),Ci,s−,(r),Ri,s(r)).\widetilde{O}_{i,s}^{(r)}=(\widetilde{A}_{i,s}^{(r)},C_{i,s}^{-,(r)},R_{i,s}^{(r)}).

The corresponding behavior joint law is gb,r​(a~∣c−)g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}) and its fitted version is g^b,r​(a~∣c−)\widehat{g}_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

As specified in the main text, historical rounds receive fitting weights based on their context-law discrepancy from the target context law. Let νz,ttr\nu_{z,t}^{\mathrm{tr}} denote the population context marginal of the resulting weighted training sample. The full training input law may also differ from the target joint input law

μz,0​(d​c−,d​a~)=νz,0​(d​c−)​gz,0​(d​a~∣c−).\mu_{z,0}(dc^{-},d\widetilde{a})=\nu_{z,0}(dc^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}).

The context weights do not automatically identify or reconstruct the joint action/exposure law. Thus the induced clipped-ratio error and the target-joint-law error must be calibrated separately, under the joint laws used by the actual score.

Predictable fitting and scoring.

For the concentration arguments, the nuisance predictions used to score network window jj must be fixed using information available before that window is scored. Accordingly, ψ^z,r\widehat{\psi}_{z,r} denotes the stored score rule for source round rr: its target joint-law fit, response-regression fit, and behavior joint-law fit are frozen before the corresponding scoring window(s). Historical scores are not retrospectively recomputed using fits that depend on later observations. If the nuisance rule is updated within a round, the fitting cutoff and stored score must instead be indexed at the window level. This is the predictability condition used in Appendix C.1. Cross-fitting alone does not establish response transport, correct specification, or target-law overlap.

Target response versus source response.

Let mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the conditional response mean under the historical source regime. The response nuisance for candidate zz targets mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}), not automatically mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}).

When zr≠zz_{r}\neq z, fitting a regression to historical responses does not by itself identify the candidate-specific response function. A sufficient special case is conditional response invariance on the relevant support:

mb,r​(a~,c−)=mz​(a~,c−).m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}).

When this equality is not assumed, the source-to-target response discrepancy must be bounded separately. It may be included in the calibrated exposure/response budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) only if that budget covers the same source regimes, target support, and historical averaging scheme. It must not be silently absorbed into a nuisance-fitting error that measures estimation under the source response law only.

Nuisance errors and the meaning of the budgets.

The response-nuisance error ϵm,t​(z)\epsilon_{m,t}(z) must control ‖m^z,r−mz‖L2​(νr,gb,r)\|\widehat{m}_{z,r}-m_{z}\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{r},g_{b,r})} under the score-law measures, uniformly over the relevant source rounds or through a separately justified historical-average bound. The quantity ϵπ,t​(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z) must control ‖w^z,r−w¯z,r‖L2​(νr,gb,r)\|\widehat{w}_{z,r}-\bar{w}_{z,r}\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{r},g_{b,r})}, where w^z,r\widehat{w}_{z,r} is the fitted clipped joint ratio and w¯z,r=min⁡{gz,0/gb,r,wmax}\bar{w}_{z,r}=\min\{g_{z,0}/g_{b,r},w_{\max}\} is its clipped oracle counterpart. A bound on the raw fitted behavior propensity alone is not sufficient unless it is shown to imply this induced-ratio bound. The target-joint-law error is first order and is accounted for by ϵ¯target,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{target},t}(z).

The context-shift term ϵ¯shift,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},t}(z) controls score averaging across source and target context laws. The configuration term ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z) controls only the calibrated context-marginal nuisance transfer described in Appendix B.10; it does not, by itself, control joint-treatment-law mismatch or conditional-response transport. The nuisance-product, target-joint-law, clipping, context, and response terms therefore have distinct roles. A response discrepancy already included in ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) must not be counted again as a configuration mismatch.

Scope of the fitting guarantees.

Configuration-aware fitting is a valid certificate component only when target-law, response-nuisance, induced-ratio, context-transport, and response-transport bounds are independently justified. Fit quality or small observed discrepancies alone do not guarantee target-law accuracy; the result remains conditional on Appendix B.6.

Appendix C Assumptions, Calibration, and Information Growth

C.1 Finite-Sample Conditions for Causal Value Certification

This appendix supplies auditable mathematical sufficient conditions for the sampling component of Theorem 1 and for its use in Theorem 3. Its statements are conditional on the identification, overlap, nuisance, and transport requirements in Appendices B.8–D.3. The target treatment unit is the joint action/exposure A~=(A,E)\widetilde{A}=(A,E), and the context used for causal scoring is the pre-action context C−C^{-}. The resulting confidence certificate combines the concentration results below with the independently calibrated target-transport bounds in Appendix B.10.

Network-window unit and predictable scoring.

Index the available network windows in observation order by j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. For candidate configuration zz, define

Yj,z=1N​∑i=1Nψ^z,j​(O~i,j),O~i,j=(A~i,j,Ci,j−,Ri,j).Y_{j,z}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\psi}_{z,j}(\widetilde{O}_{i,j}),\qquad\widetilde{O}_{i,j}=(\widetilde{A}_{i,j},C^{-}_{i,j},R_{i,j}).

Here A~i,j\widetilde{A}_{i,j} is the observed joint action/exposure treatment unit and Ci,j−C^{-}_{i,j} contains only information available strictly before the focal action.

The nuisance fits, fitted behavior joint law, and candidate scoring function used at window jj are measurable with respect to a pre-window sigma field ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}. A strictly forward, block-separated nuisance-training protocol satisfies this predictable-fit condition and preserves the temporal ordering required by the concentration argument. The within-window dependence among nodes is otherwise unrestricted by the martingale statement below. By the clipped-score range, |Yj,z|≤Bψ|Y_{j,z}|\leq B_{\psi}. The network-window count nn, rather than the total number N​nNn of dependent node-level records, is the unit in the following concentration arguments.

Lemma 2 (Finite-sample martingale route).

Fix a candidate zz and assume the predictable-fit condition above. For every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

ℙ⁡(|1n​∑j=1n[Yj,z−𝔼⁡(Yj,z∣ℱj−1)]|>2​Bψ​2​log⁡(2/α)n)≤α.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left[Y_{j,z}-\mathbb{E}(Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})\right]\right|>2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\alpha)}{n}}\right)\leq\alpha. (39)

No independence or mixing assumption across windows is needed for this centered martingale statement. It does not control the predictable-mean drift.

Proof.

The summands are martingale differences bounded in absolute value by 2​Bψ2B_{\psi}. Azuma–Hoeffding and a two-sided union bound give

2​exp⁡(−x28​n​Bψ2)2\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{8nB_{\psi}^{2}}\right)

as an upper bound on the probability that the absolute centered sum exceeds xx. Setting

x=2​Bψ​2​n​log⁡(2/α)x=2B_{\psi}\sqrt{2n\log(2/\alpha)}

and dividing by nn yields Eq. (39). ∎

Calibrating predictable bias and stochastic fluctuation.

For each window, condition on ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1} and use the conditional behavior and context laws in the exact nuisance and transport decomposition of Appendix B.8. Let

Δj,zpred=𝔼⁡(Yj,z∣ℱj−1)−W∞​(z,0)\Delta^{\mathrm{pred}}_{j,z}=\mathbb{E}(Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})-W_{\infty}(z;0)

denote the total signed predictable-mean discrepancy, distinct from the predictable-window drift term in the second line of Eq. (60). The following is a sufficient pathwise budget requirement on an event 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

|1n​∑j=1nΔj,zpred|≤ϵm,t​(z)​ϵπ,t​(z)+ϵ¯target,t​(z)+ϵclip,t​(z)+ϵexp​(z)+ϵ¯shift,t​(z)+ϵ¯cfg,t​(z)+κ^t​(z).\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Delta^{\mathrm{pred}}_{j,z}\right|\leq\epsilon_{m,t}(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{target},t}(z)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},t}(z)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{shift},t}(z)+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{cfg},t}(z)+\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z). (40)

For this inequality to hold, each budget on the right-hand side must be calibrated for the relevant joint action/exposure laws, source regimes, and historical-window averaging scheme.

In particular, ϵm,t​(z)\epsilon_{m,t}(z) and ϵπ,t​(z)\epsilon_{\pi,t}(z) must control, respectively, ‖m^z,r−mz‖L2​(νr,gb,r)\|\widehat{m}_{z,r}-m_{z}\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{r},g_{b,r})} and ‖w^z,r−w¯z,r‖L2​(νr,gb,r)\|\widehat{w}_{z,r}-\bar{w}_{z,r}\|_{L_{2}(\nu_{r},g_{b,r})} for the source-window score laws, uniformly over the source rounds in the prefix or through a separately justified bound on the averaged products. The latter is an induced clipped joint-ratio error; a raw behavior-propensity estimation error is sufficient only if a valid inequality transfers it to this ratio norm. The clipping allowance must cover the clipping contributions appearing in the actual proof decomposition, and the target-joint-law term must control the first-order error in the fitted target joint distribution.

The main-text exposure/response budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) must dominate the historical average of both the score-level response residual in Eq. (62) and the target-context response discrepancy in Eq. (31), as well as any exposure-representation error not already included in those quantities. This is a calibration requirement for the actual stored scoring rules and admissible source regimes; the target-context bound in Eq. (31) alone does not establish it. A uniform bound over source regimes and prefixes is sufficient, while a direct bound on the combined contribution in the exact telescope may be tighter. These component bounds are folded into the single ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) term and must not be added a second time as separate terms in ϵ¯tot,t​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z).

The context-shift allowance must apply to the source and target context laws and the source-response functional actually used in the historical average. The configuration-mismatch allowance is the calibrated context-marginal nuisance-transfer term defined in Appendix B.10. It does not, by itself, control joint action/exposure input-law mismatch or conditional response transport. The direct nuisance bounds must therefore be calibrated under the actual score-law measures, or any further transfer must be separately justified. A response discrepancy already included in ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) must not be counted again as a configuration-mismatch term.

Equation (40) is a sufficient calibration requirement, not a bound inferred from stationarity or an empirical block-drift statistic. It must be justified using the target-law, clipping, nuisance, exposure/response-transport, and context-law conditions in Appendices B.8–D.3. One sufficient route is to bound the window-averaged contributions of each of the four non-statistical terms in Eq. (60).

Proposition 2 (Concrete conditional simultaneous certificate).

Suppose 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is finite with M=|𝒵|M=|\mathcal{Z}|, and ℙ⁡(𝒢)≥1−δ/2\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G})\geq 1-\delta/2, where on 𝒢\mathcal{G} Eq. (40) holds simultaneously for every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. Suppose the estimators use nn network windows and the predictable-fit condition holds for every candidate. Define

comp⁡(𝒵)=log⁡M\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})=\log M

and suppose the certified statistical effective information count satisfies

0<n¯eff,t​(z)≤n/4,z∈𝒵.0<\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)\leq n/4,\qquad z\in\mathcal{Z}. (41)

Then the bound in Theorem 1, with the same stated 2​Bψ2B_{\psi} statistical coefficient, holds simultaneously for every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Proof.

Apply Lemma 2 with α=δ/(2​M)\alpha=\delta/(2M) and take a union bound over the MM candidates. The resulting sampling failure probability is at most δ/2\delta/2, and the stochastic radius for each candidate is

2​Bψ​2​log⁡(4​M/δ)n.2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4M/\delta)}{n}}.

Write

L=log⁡M+log⁡(2/δ).L=\log M+\log(2/\delta).

Since L≥log⁡2L\geq\log 2,

log⁡(4​M/δ)=L+log⁡2≤2​L.\log(4M/\delta)=L+\log 2\leq 2L.

Consequently,

2​Bψ​2​log⁡(4​M/δ)n≤2​Bψ​Ln/4≤2​Bψ​Ln¯eff,t​(z).2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4M/\delta)}{n}}\leq 2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{L}{n/4}}\leq 2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{L}{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)}}.

The last inequality follows from n¯eff,t​(z)≤n/4\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)\leq n/4. Intersect this simultaneous sampling event with 𝒢\mathcal{G} and apply Eq. (40). The total failure probability is at most δ\delta. ∎

Alternative mixing/block-coupling route.

When nuisance scoring is fixed separately from a stationary evaluation stream and a conditional absolute-regularity bound is supplied, independent-block coupling provides an alternative finite-sample certificate. This route requires its own dependence assumptions and does not follow merely from the martingale result above.

Lemma 3 (Block-coupled sampling route).

Let Y1,…,YnY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} be a bounded sequence with |Yj|≤Bψ|Y_{j}|\leq B_{\psi}, stationary conditional on a separate fitting sigma field, and with absolute-regularity coefficient β⁡(k)\beta(k). Choose integers q,m≥1q,m\geq 1 such that n=2​m​q+rn=2mq+r, 0≤r<2​q0\leq r<2q, and suppose 2​m​β​(q)≤α/22m\beta(q)\leq\alpha/2. Then, conditional on the fitting field, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha,

|1n​∑j=1nYj−𝔼​Y1|≤Bψ​2​log⁡(8/α)m+4​Bψ​qn.\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{j}-\mathbb{E}Y_{1}\right|\leq B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(8/\alpha)}{m}}+\frac{4B_{\psi}q}{n}. (42)

In particular, if β(q)≤Cβexp(−q/τ)\beta(q)\leq C_{\beta}\exp(-q/\tau) with known constants and qq is chosen to satisfy the coupling condition, the right-hand side is fully specified. One sufficient choice is

q≥τ​log⁡(4​Cβ​n/α),q\geq\tau\log(4C_{\beta}n/\alpha),

provided n≥2​qn\geq 2q.

Proof.

Partition the first 2​m​q2mq observations into 2​m2m successive blocks of length qq. Form the mm odd-indexed and mm even-indexed block averages. Blocks within each parity group are separated by at least qq observations. The absolute-regularity coupling bound controls the probability that either group differs from its independent block coupling by at most 2​m​β​(q)≤α/22m\beta(q)\leq\alpha/2.

Conditional on successful coupling, each parity group consists of mm independent block averages bounded in absolute value by BψB_{\psi}. Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over the two groups give the stated stochastic radius with additional failure probability at most α/2\alpha/2. The rr omitted observations change the full sample mean relative to the mean of the first 2​m​q2mq observations by at most

2​Bψ​rn≤4​Bψ​qn.\frac{2B_{\psi}r}{n}\leq\frac{4B_{\psi}q}{n}.

Combining these bounds proves Eq. (42). ∎

Configuration covers and complete failure accounting.

For infinite compact 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, a finite ε\varepsilon-net can be used only if the evaluated estimator and the target value are uniformly LZL_{Z}-Lipschitz on the relevant confidence event. The lift from net points requires a 2​LZ​ε2L_{Z}\varepsilon additive remainder, which must be included in the stated approximation/error budget. The local 1−δ1-\delta conclusion above is for one evaluation time. For the adaptive online algorithm, choose positive δt\delta_{t} satisfying

∑t=2Tδt≤δ\sum_{t=2}^{T}\delta_{t}\leq\delta

and allocate each δt\delta_{t} among sampling, nuisance/transport calibration, and any covering event. A uniform-in-round guarantee does not follow from repeating a fixed-round confidence interval without this allocation.

Effective information and drift calibration.

The operational shrinkage proxy (20) is diagnostic only. The theorem uses a validated lower-information bound, such as Eq. (41) or a calibrated block-coupling counterpart, and not the proxy by itself. The adjacent-block statistic (21) is similarly usable as a drift allowance only when validated against the predictable-bias condition Eq. (40). These distinct inputs capture complementary features of post-burn-in data: effective information and residual predictable-mean drift. Independent calibration, model-dependent deviation bounds, or conservative deterministic bounds provide sufficient conditions. The slow-mixing family in Appendix D.4 clarifies their role.

Limited-overlap local-action calibration example.

Under a correct known local-action mixture

bA=(1−η)​pA+η​ξ,η<1,b_{A}=(1-\eta)p_{A}+\eta\xi,\qquad\eta<1,

the target local-action law can be recovered as

pA=bA−η​ξ1−η,p_{A}=\frac{b_{A}-\eta\xi}{1-\eta},

provided the equality defines a valid probability vector. A fitted version obeys

‖p^A−pA‖1=11−η​‖b^A−bA‖1\|\widehat{p}_{A}-p_{A}\|_{1}=\frac{1}{1-\eta}\|\widehat{b}_{A}-b_{A}\|_{1}

when the fitted quantities satisfy the same mixture relation. Thus an independently validated confidence bound on the local-action probabilities yields a corresponding local-action error bound.

This inversion does not, by itself, recover the target joint action/exposure law gz,0g_{z,0} from the marginal local-action law. A joint-law reconstruction requires the actual joint action-generation mechanism, including dependencies among contemporaneous actions and the exposure mapping. At η=1\eta=1, the mixture inversion does not identify the target local-action law pAp_{A}. Moreover, even a known target local-action law does not identify the counterfactual context distribution νz,0\nu_{z,0} from arbitrary exploratory logs. Calibrated joint-treatment, exposure, and context- transport conditions therefore remain separate requirements.

C.2 Calibrated Error Budgets and Information Growth

This appendix develops two components of the causal decision guarantee: finite-sample calibration of target-value bias terms and growth of certified information along the selected configuration sequence. Independent audit observations provide explicit upper bounds for the identification and transport budgets; per-visit information conditions then yield the square-root summability used by Theorem 3. The construction gives operational interpretations to the sufficient conditions in Theorems 1 and 3.

C.2.1 Target identification and observational equivalence

Proposition 3 (Observational indistinguishability).

Without identifying restrictions or independent information about the no-exploration action law, the target-policy bias cannot have a uniformly vanishing, data-dependent high-probability bound based only on exploratory logs. The same conclusion applies to the full target certificate.

Proof.

Take one context, two actions A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\}, and deterministic reward R=AR=A. Suppose the only logged regime is η=1\eta=1 with known exploration law ξ⁡(1)=1/2\xi(1)=1/2. Consider two admissible target laws p+​(1)=1p_{+}(1)=1 and p−​(1)=0p_{-}(1)=0. In both environments the observed law is A∼Ber⁡(1/2)A\sim\mathrm{Ber}(1/2) and R=AR=A, independently of the target law. Yet the no-exploration values are W+=1W_{+}=1 and W−=0W_{-}=0. Under the common law of the observed data, any interval I⁡(D)I(D) having coverage at least 1−δ1-\delta for both targets must contain both 00 and 11 simultaneously with probability at least 1−2​δ1-2\delta; on that event its width is at least 11. Thus no shrinking uniformly valid target certificate can be deduced from these logs. The construction is also an exact failure case for inversion of the mixture b=(1−η)​p+η​ξb=(1-\eta)p+\eta\xi at η=1\eta=1. ∎

No statement here rules out identification when η<1\eta<1, the known mixture model is correct, and sufficiently informative observations are available. It rules out treating fitted target policies, enriched-exposure sensitivity, or empirical IPMs as automatically certified upper bounds.

A separate context-shift obstruction can persist even for a fixed 0<η<10<\eta<1 if no structural relation between the context laws νz,η\nu_{z,\eta} and νz,0\nu_{z,0} is assumed: take a logging context C≡0C\equiv 0 and reward R≡0R\equiv 0 in two systems at that positive exploration rate, but let the unobserved no-exploration regime have C≡1C\equiv 1 and deterministic target reward θ∈{0,1}\theta\in\{0,1\}. The two logging laws coincide and the two target values differ by one. This counterexample is deliberately excluded when a verified transport condition links the regimes; its purpose is to show why that condition cannot be inferred from logged outcomes alone.

Finally, assume the expected bounded score in each evaluation window is at total variation distance at most dj,zd_{j,z} from the corresponding reference score law, where dj,zd_{j,z} has a known simultaneous upper bound. Then
