An adjacent-block empirical difference alone does not imply this contraction or certify its constants.

Proposition 4 (Finite-audit value certificate).

Suppose all finite-state audit and conditional-response identification assumptions above hold, the predictable network-window scoring condition of Lemma 2 holds, and the target value has the decomposition in Eq. (60). Replace the bias budgets in Theorem 1 by the componentwise upper bounds in Eqs. (46), (49), and (50). Set the audit level to α=δ/2\alpha=\delta/2 and allocate the remaining δ/2\delta/2 to the centered-score event. Then the resulting simultaneous value certificate holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta for all MM configurations at that evaluation time. For an adaptive run, the failure allocation must be repeated with roundwise levels whose sum is at most the global δ\delta.

Proof.

The audit concentration event and the majorants in Eqs. (45)–(49) control the target joint-law, response nuisance, induced ratio, clipping, context-shift, configuration, and score-level response-transport contributions simultaneously. The stated total-variation envelope bounds the remaining predictable post-burn-in drift by Eq. (50). Substituting these bounds into the exact telescope in Eq. (60) verifies the pathwise bias condition in Eq. (40). The centered-score concentration result then supplies the sampling part of the certificate. For a full adaptive run, allocate the failure budget across rounds so that the total remains at most δ\delta. ∎

Calibration interfaces and implementation.

This finite-state construction is deliberately strong: it requires independent audits of the full joint action/exposure cells, source-regime responses, target responses, and context laws. It does not derive a joint propensity from marginal local-action propensities. If these audits or structural restrictions are unavailable, the corresponding error budget is uncertified rather than zero.

C.2.3 Selected-configuration information growth

Let Nz​(t−1)N_{z}(t-1) count qualifying post-initialization visits to zz strictly before decision tt. Merely defining an empirical or conservative-looking n¯eff,t−1​(z)\underline{n}_{\rm eff,t-1}(z) does not force it to grow on such visits.

Lemma 4 (Per-visit lower information bound).

Suppose there are M<∞M<\infty configurations. After at most HH initialization decisions, every selected configuration receives a predictable, valid score, and its certified predecision information count satisfies

n¯eff,t−1​(zt)≥λ⁡(1+Nzt​(t−1)),λ>0,\underline{n}_{\rm eff,t-1}(z_{t})\geq\lambda\bigl(1+N_{z_{t}}(t-1)\bigr),\qquad\lambda>0, (51)

for each noninitialization decision tt. Then for any adaptive sequence of configuration selections,

∑t​ noninitialization1n¯eff,t−1​(zt)≤2​M​Tλ.\sum_{t\text{ noninitialization}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\underline{n}_{\rm eff,t-1}(z_{t})}}\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{MT}{\lambda}}. (52)

In particular, when each eligible visit contributes at least s≥1s\geq 1 new nonreused network windows and the martingale information certificate is constructed as n¯eff=n/4\underline{n}_{\rm eff}=n/4, the condition follows with λ=s/4\lambda=s/4 after providing one certified pilot score per configuration and preserving all subsequent evaluated windows.

Proof.

For a given configuration, index its qualifying selections by k=1,…,Nz​(T)k=1,\dots,N_{z}(T). By Eq. (51), its kkth contribution is at most 1/λ​k1/\sqrt{\lambda k}. Thus

∑k=1Nz​(T)1λ​k≤2λ​Nz​(T).\sum_{k=1}^{N_{z}(T)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda k}}\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\sqrt{N_{z}(T)}.

Summing over configurations and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields ∑zNz​(T)≤M​∑zNz​(T)≤M​T\sum_{z}\sqrt{N_{z}(T)}\leq\sqrt{M\sum_{z}N_{z}(T)}\leq\sqrt{MT}. This proof permits fully adaptive configuration selection; it does not require a uniform lower bound on the number of times each arm is chosen. ∎

Corollary 2 (An explicit conditional regret bound).

Under the simultaneous certified-value event of Theorem 1 and the information-growth assumption (51), write LT=comp⁡(𝒵)+log⁡(2​T/δ)L_{T}=\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})+\log(2T/\delta) and Et​(z)=ϵ¯tot,t​(z)+κ^t​(z)E_{t}(z)=\bar{\epsilon}_{\rm tot,t}(z)+\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z). Then

RegT≤2​Bu​H+8​Bψ​M​T​LTλ+2​∑t​ noninitializationEt−1​(zt).\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq 2B_{u}H+8B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{MTL_{T}}{\lambda}}+2\sum_{t\text{ noninitialization}}E_{t-1}(z_{t}). (53)

For fixed MM and λ\lambda, the stochastic term is O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}). When MM varies, the dependence M\sqrt{M} cannot be dropped from this counting argument.

Proof.

Every initial decision loses at most 2​Bu2B_{u}. On the joint confidence event, optimism as in Appendix D.5 gives instantaneous regret at most twice the predecision radius. For every noninitialization decision this is at most 4​Bψ​LT/n¯eff,t−1​(zt)+2​Et−1​(zt)4B_{\psi}\sqrt{L_{T}/\underline{n}_{\rm eff,t-1}(z_{t})}+2E_{t-1}(z_{t}). Apply Lemma 4 and add the initialization regret. ∎

Proposition 5 (Growth does not follow from OFU alone).

Algorithm 4.4, without a condition ensuring at least one newly usable, certified scoring window per eligible deployment, does not imply Eq. (51) or its summability conclusion.

Proof.

Consider a configuration repeatedly deployed under a law that never provides the support required to fit its target-policy or response nuisance. Its post-burn-in window count grows, but its number of certifiable evaluation windows may remain zero. More generally, n¯eff,t​(z)≡1\underline{n}_{\rm eff,t}(z)\equiv 1 is a conservative lower-information number for an increasing amount of independent data, and nothing in the original OFU selection rule rules out retaining that constant certificate. If such an arm is repeatedly chosen, the predecision reciprocal-square-root sum is Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T), not O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}). OFU controls selection given confidence radii; it does not create valid statistical information by itself. ∎

Implementation of information-growth checks.

The implementation records scored network windows and predecision information counts. The quantity n/4n/4 serves as a sampling-information proxy; to apply the counting lemma, each eligible visit is checked for positive score production and the certified lower-information condition. This diagnostic connects the observed evaluation stream with the information-growth condition used in the regret analysis.

C.3 Identification, Calibration Sources, and Information-Growth Scope

This appendix collects the interpretation of assumptions already used in Theorems 1–3. It is a scope and implementation clarification, not an additional general certification theorem. The finite-state independent-audit construction and the per-visit counting argument already appear in the existing technical appendices; neither should be confused with a guarantee based solely on uncalibrated exploratory telemetry.

C.3.1 Why correcting the local-action propensity is insufficient

Fix zz and an exploratory regime η>0\eta>0. Write bz,η​(a∣c−)b_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-}) for the observed conditional law of the focal local action and pz​(a∣c−)=πz,0​(a∣c−)p_{z}(a\mid c^{-})=\pi_{z,0}(a\mid c^{-}) for its target marginal law. Under the stated known local-action mixture,

bz,η​(a∣c−)=(1−η)​pz​(a∣c−)+η​ξ​(a∣c−).b_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})=(1-\eta)p_{z}(a\mid c^{-})+\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-}).

When η<1\eta<1, ξ\xi is known, and the mixture identity is valid at the conditioned contexts, the marginal action law can be recovered by

pz​(a∣c−)=bz,η​(a∣c−)−η​ξ​(a∣c−)1−η.p_{z}(a\mid c^{-})=\frac{b_{z,\eta}(a\mid c^{-})-\eta\xi(a\mid c^{-})}{1-\eta}.

Estimation error in bz,ηb_{z,\eta} is amplified by 1/(1−η)1/(1-\eta), and the identity becomes nonidentifying at η=1\eta=1. This inversion does not recover the no-exploration steady-state context law νz,0\nu_{z,0}. More importantly for the main theorem, it does not in general recover the target joint action/exposure law gz,0​(a~∣c−)g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}). The latter depends on the actual joint action-generation mechanism, including dependencies among contemporaneous neighboring actions and the exposure mapping. It must be identified or calibrated from that mechanism or from an independent joint-cell audit; it cannot be inferred from the marginal local-action mixture alone.

To display the two transport issues in the general notation, let mb,r​(a~,c−)m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) denote the conditional response under a historical source regime and mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) the target-regime response. Define the joint-action-corrected source value

Vz,rjoint​corrected:=𝔼C−∼νzr,ηr​∫𝒜~gz,0​(𝑑a~∣C−)​mb,r​(a~,C−).V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{joint\ corrected}}:=\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}}}\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},C^{-}).

Even if joint-treatment weighting is exact, the source and target responses may differ. For bounded |mb,r|,|mz|≤Bu|m_{b,r}|,|m_{z}|\leq B_{u}, a useful upper bound is

|Vz,rjoint​corrected−W∞​(z,0)|≤\displaystyle\left|V_{z,r}^{\mathrm{joint\ corrected}}-W_{\infty}(z;0)\right|\leq{} Bu​‖νzr,ηr−νz,0‖1\displaystyle B_{u}\left\|\nu_{z_{r},\eta_{r}}-\nu_{z,0}\right\|_{1}
+𝔼C−∼νz,0∫𝒜~gz,0(da~∣C−)|mb,r(a~,C−)−mz(a~,C−)|,\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})|m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})-m_{z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})|, (54)

where ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} denotes the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance between context probability vectors. The first term is context transport, and the second is conditional-response transport. Both require an identifying restriction or an independently supported bound; neither follows from improved marginal action overlap.

C.3.2 Data sources and audit cost for Theorem 1

A valid application of the general certificate must supply joint, predecision error bounds, rather than substitute an empirical proxy for a high-probability upper bound. Examples of sufficient sources are:

Certificate component Sufficient source or restriction
Target joint-treatment law gz,0g_{z,0} Independent joint action/exposure-cell audit, or a verified joint action-generation model. A marginal local-action mixture is sufficient only when the induced joint-law identity is separately proved.
No-exploration context νz,0\nu_{z,0} Target-regime context audit, or a proven structural transport bound. Exploratory propensity overlap alone is insufficient.
Target-regime conditional response mz​(a~,c−)m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) Identified interventional audit of the target response, or an explicit regime-invariance/exposure-sufficiency assumption with a certified approximation allowance.
Clipping and nuisance error Joint-support bounds and fitted-model validation on independent or appropriately buffered evaluation data, including a bound on the induced clipped joint-ratio error.
Network dependence and drift Predictable-score martingale conditions, independently validated mixing or block-coupling constants, and a justified drift envelope; an empirical autocorrelation is not by itself a certificate.

The finite-state audit constructions provide examples of these sources under strong sampling and identification assumptions. When a required joint-treatment audit cell or structural restriction is unavailable, the corresponding budget is uncertified, not zero; Theorem 1 then does not supply an operational finite-sample coverage claim.

Any operator-collected pilot or audit windows used to learn νz,0\nu_{z,0} or the target-regime response must be counted in the operational measurement budget. For audit deployments 𝒜\mathcal{A}, one can record separately their measurement-induced loss and any configuration-selection loss as

Daudit\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{audit}} =∑r∈𝒜{W∞​(zr,0)−W∞​(zr,ηr)},\displaystyle=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{A}}\{W_{\infty}(z_{r};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{r};\eta_{r})\}, (55)
Raudit\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{audit}} =∑r∈𝒜{W∞​(z⋆,0)−W∞​(zr,0)}.\displaystyle=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{A}}\{W_{\infty}(z^{\star};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{r};0)\}. (56)

These expressions are accounting definitions, not additional lower bounds. If independent target-regime audits are supplied externally, their data-collection cost must instead be disclosed separately. In the paper’s restricted matched-reward construction, such target-regime audits are not required because the relevant target value has a known identifiable form.

C.3.3 Anytime validity and a concrete sufficient growth condition

For a finite evaluation horizon, allocate failure probabilities δt>0\delta_{t}>0 such that ∑tδt≤δ\sum_{t}\delta_{t}\leq\delta and divide each δt\delta_{t} across the centered-score event, calibration, coupling, and drift conditions actually invoked. A fixed-round certificate at level 1−δ1-\delta cannot simply be reused without adjustment after data-dependent online selection.

For the finite candidate set, write Nz​(t−1)N_{z}(t-1) for the number of qualifying past deployments of configuration zz. One sufficient condition, already established through the counting argument in the existing information-growth appendix, is that outside at most HH initialization rounds there exists a fixed λ>0\lambda>0 such that

n¯eff,t−1​(zt)≥λ⁡{1+Nzt​(t−1)}for each eligible ​t.\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z_{t})\geq\lambda\{1+N_{z_{t}}(t-1)\}\quad\text{for each eligible }t. (57)

Then a pathwise counting argument gives

∑t​eligible1n¯eff,t−1​(zt)≤2​|𝒵|​Tλ.\sum_{t\ \mathrm{eligible}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z_{t})}}\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{Z}|T}{\lambda}}.

Combined with a valid simultaneous confidence event and certified bias budgets et−1​(zt)e_{t-1}(z_{t}), the standard OFU argument yields a conditional bound of the form

RegT≤2​Bu​H+O⁡(Bψ​|𝒵|​T​[comp⁡(𝒵)+log⁡(T/δ)]λ)+2​∑t​eligibleet−1​(zt).\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq 2B_{u}H+O\!\left(B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{Z}|T[\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})+\log(T/\delta)]}{\lambda}}\right)+2\sum_{t\ \mathrm{eligible}}e_{t-1}(z_{t}).

This repeats the logical implication already present in the information-growth appendix. OFU does not imply (57): it must be supported by certified scoring-window production, overlap, and the dependence model. A measurement schedule can enforce overlap only when its action and context-support assumptions have been verified. Without such a route, regret convergence remains a conditional guarantee.

Relation to the identification–deployment lower bound.

Theorem 2 is a minimax lower-bound construction with potentially horizon-dependent mixing time, whereas Theorem 3 is an upper-bound implication under calibration and selected-information growth. Their assumptions and loss criteria do not currently supply a matched Pareto lower/upper bound on one common model class. Such a matching result would require additional algorithmic and theoretical analysis; it is not claimed here.

Appendix D Full Proofs and Decision-Theoretic Guarantees

D.1 Fixed-Configuration Concentration

Fix a candidate configuration zz and an evaluation round tt. Use the network-window score sequence Yj,zY_{j,z} and count Jt=T0​tJ_{t}=T_{0}t defined in Appendix B.4. Each Yj,zY_{j,z} is the within-window average of the node-level clipped DR scores, so |Yj,z|≤Bψ|Y_{j,z}|\leq B_{\psi} without assuming independence among nodes in the same window. The stored score rule is predictable with respect to the pre-window filtration ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}.

Define the predictable-score average

Y¯tpred​(z)=1Jt​∑j=1Jt𝔼⁡[Yj,z∣ℱj−1].\bar{Y}_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}(z)=\frac{1}{J_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t}}\mathbb{E}[Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}].

The martingale-difference route gives, for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

ℙ⁡(|W^t​(z,0)−Y¯tpred​(z)|>2​Bψ​2​log⁡(2/α)Jt)≤α.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0)-\bar{Y}_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}(z)\right|>2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\alpha)}{J_{t}}}\right)\leq\alpha. (58)

No independence or mixing assumption across network windows is needed for this centered martingale statement. It does not, however, bound the predictable-mean discrepancy |Y¯tpred​(z)−W∞​(z,0)||\bar{Y}_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}(z)-W_{\infty}(z;0)|. That discrepancy is controlled separately by the calibrated identification, nuisance, transport, and drift budgets in Appendices D.3 and C.1.

For compatibility with the main-text radius, suppose the certified information count satisfies

0<n¯eff,t​(z)≤Jt/4.0<\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)\leq J_{t}/4.

Then Eq. (58) implies the conservative bound

ℙ⁡(|W^t​(z,0)−Y¯tpred​(z)|>2​Bψ​log⁡(2/α)n¯eff,t​(z))≤α.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left|\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0)-\bar{Y}_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}(z)\right|>2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\alpha)}{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)}}\right)\leq\alpha. (59)

The inequality follows because n¯eff,t​(z)≤Jt/4\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z)\leq J_{t}/4 makes the displayed radius at least as large as the Azuma–Hoeffding radius. A valid bound on the predictable-mean discrepancy must then be added to obtain a value certificate. The operational ESS shrinkage proxy in Appendix B.4 is diagnostic only; it cannot replace the certified lower-information count.

An alternative block-coupling route is available when the score sequence is stationary conditional on a separate fitting field and a valid absolute-regularity envelope is supplied. In that case, use the explicit block-coupled inequality in Lemma 3 of Appendix C.1. A block-coupling radius is not implied by an empirical autocorrelation estimate alone.

D.2 Uniformization over the Configuration Space

Let 𝒞ε\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon} be a finite ε\varepsilon-cover of the configuration space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, with cardinality 𝒩⁡(ε,𝒵)\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Z}). At every net point, apply the fixed-configuration certificate with failure probability δ/𝒩⁡(ε,𝒵)\delta/\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Z}), allocating that probability among the centered-score and calibration events actually used. A union bound gives a simultaneous event on which

maxz′∈𝒞ε⁡|W^t​(z′,0)−W∞​(z′,0)|≤maxz′∈𝒞ε⁡{2​Bψ​log⁡(2​𝒩​(ε,𝒵)/δ)n¯eff,t​(z′)+ϵ¯tot,t​(z′)+κ^t​(z′)},\max_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}}|\widehat{W}_{t}(z^{\prime};0)-W_{\infty}(z^{\prime};0)|\leq\max_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}}\left\{2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Z})/\delta)}{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t}(z^{\prime})}}+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t}(z^{\prime})+\widehat{\kappa}_{t}(z^{\prime})\right\},

provided the componentwise calibration conditions of Theorem 1 hold at all net points.

If both W^t​(⋅,0)\widehat{W}_{t}(\cdot;0) and W∞​(⋅,0)W_{\infty}(\cdot;0) are uniformly LZL_{Z}-Lipschitz on the relevant confidence event, every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} has a net point z′z^{\prime} with d⁡(z,z′)≤εd(z,z^{\prime})\leq\varepsilon, and

|W^t​(z,0)−W∞​(z,0)|≤|W^t​(z′,0)−W∞​(z′,0)|+2​LZ​ε.|\widehat{W}_{t}(z;0)-W_{\infty}(z;0)|\leq|\widehat{W}_{t}(z^{\prime};0)-W_{\infty}(z^{\prime};0)|+2L_{Z}\varepsilon.

Thus the cover adds the explicit remainder 2​LZ​ε2L_{Z}\varepsilon, which must be included in the approximation/error budget. Neither the union bound nor a finite cover establishes the Lipschitz condition or the identification and transport budgets. For this argument, comp⁡(𝒵)\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z}) may be taken as log⁡𝒩⁡(ε,𝒵)\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Z}), with the covering remainder reported separately.

D.3 Proof of Theorem 1: Conditional Certificate

Fix a predecision round t≥2t\geq 2 and a candidate configuration zz. Flatten the historical post-burn-in network windows available before round tt into a time-ordered sequence j=1,…,Jt−1j=1,\ldots,J_{t-1}, where

Jt−1=(t−1)​T0.J_{t-1}=(t-1)T_{0}.

Let (r⁡(j),s⁡(j))(r(j),s(j)) denote the deployment round and within-round window corresponding to index jj, and write

O~i,j=(A~i,j,Ci,j−,Ri,j),A~i,j=(Ai,j,Ei,j).\widetilde{O}_{i,j}=\bigl(\widetilde{A}_{i,j},C^{-}_{i,j},R_{i,j}\bigr),\qquad\widetilde{A}_{i,j}=(A_{i,j},E_{i,j}).

Here Ci,j−C^{-}_{i,j} contains only information available strictly before the focal action, while A~i,j\widetilde{A}_{i,j} denotes the observed joint action/exposure treatment unit.

Let ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1} denote the information available before scoring window jj. The nuisance predictions, fitted behavior joint law, and scoring rule used for that window are ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}-measurable. This predictable, prequential convention is required for the filtration-based concentration argument below.

Define the network-window score

Yj,z=1N​∑i=1Nψ^j,z​(O~i,j),W^t−1​(z,0)=1Jt−1​∑j=1Jt−1Yj,z.Y_{j,z}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\psi}_{j,z}(\widetilde{O}_{i,j}),\qquad\widehat{W}_{t-1}(z;0)=\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}Y_{j,z}.

The score ψ^j,z\widehat{\psi}_{j,z} is the stored prequential score rule for this window. The target-law and response fits used inside it are frozen before the window is scored, and the behavior joint law is the fit for source round r⁡(j)r(j). The fitting-cutoff indices are suppressed inside the main-text notation ψ^z,r\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}. This is exactly the main-text normalization:

W^t−1​(z,0)=1N​T0​(t−1)​∑r=1t−1∑s=1T0∑i=1Nψ^z,r​(O~i,s(r)).\widehat{W}_{t-1}(z;0)=\frac{1}{NT_{0}(t-1)}\sum_{r=1}^{t-1}\sum_{s=1}^{T_{0}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\psi}_{z,r}(\widetilde{O}_{i,s}^{(r)}).

Thus Jt−1J_{t-1} counts network windows, whereas N​Jt−1NJ_{t-1} counts node-level records. The concentration argument treats the aggregated network-window scores as its time-ordered units and does not assume independence among nodes within a window.

Reference laws and transported responses.

For each historical window jj, let Pz,jevalP_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}} denote the corresponding post-burn-in reference evaluation law for the stored score of candidate zz. Its source context marginal is νzr⁡(j),ηr⁡(j)\nu_{z_{r(j)},\eta_{r(j)}}, and its conditional joint action/exposure law is denoted by gb,r⁡(j)(⋅∣C−)g_{b,r(j)}(\cdot\mid C^{-}). Expectations under this law hold the fitted scoring rule fixed. The difference between the actual conditional score mean and this reference-law mean is handled separately as predictable-window drift.

Let mb,r⁡(j)​(a~,c−)m_{b,r(j)}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}) be the source-regime conditional response mean, and define

Vj,zlog​(c−)=∫𝒜~mb,r⁡(j)​(a~,c−)​gz,0​(𝑑a~∣c−),V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(c^{-})=\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}m_{b,r(j)}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})g_{z,0}(d\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

where gz,0g_{z,0} is the target joint action/exposure law without measurement exploration. This definition presumes that the source response is meaningful on the relevant target support and that the corresponding transport conditions are satisfied.

The deviation admits the following exact decomposition:

W^t−1​(z,0)−W∞​(z,0)=\displaystyle\widehat{W}_{t-1}(z;0)-W_{\infty}(z;0)={} 1Jt−1​∑j=1Jt−1[Yj,z−𝔼⁡[Yj,z∣ℱj−1]]\displaystyle\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[Y_{j,z}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]\right]
+1Jt−1∑j=1Jt−1[𝔼[Yj,z∣ℱj−1]−𝔼Pz,jevalψ^j,z]\displaystyle+\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[\mathbb{E}[Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}\widehat{\psi}_{j,z}\right]
+1Jt−1∑j=1Jt−1[𝔼Pz,jevalψ^j,z−𝔼Pz,jevalVj,zlog(C−)]\displaystyle+\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}\widehat{\psi}_{j,z}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})\right]
+1Jt−1∑j=1Jt−1[𝔼Pz,jevalVj,zlog(C−)−𝔼C−∼νz,0Vj,zlog(C−)]\displaystyle+\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})-\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})\right]
+1Jt−1∑j=1Jt−1[𝔼C−∼νz,0Vj,zlog(C−)−W∞(z;0)].\displaystyle+\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})-W_{\infty}(z;0)\right]. (60)
First term: stochastic fluctuation.

The first term is the centered fluctuation of the historical network-window scores. It is controlled by the validated conditional concentration inequality under the dependence assumptions of Appendix D.1, using the effective sample size calibrated for the sequence {Yj,z}\{Y_{j,z}\}. The bound must apply to the actual predictably fitted score sequence; empirical autocorrelation alone does not establish the required concentration event.

Second term: predictable-window drift.

The second term accounts for discrepancies between the conditional score means and their reference evaluation-law counterparts. Define the signed predictable discrepancy

dj,z=𝔼⁡[Yj,z∣ℱj−1]−𝔼Pz,jeval​ψ^j,z.d_{j,z}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{j,z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}\widehat{\psi}_{j,z}.

Its contribution must be bounded by the independently justified drift allowance. In particular, the required pathwise calibration is

|1Jt−1​∑j=1Jt−1dj,z|≤κ^t−1​(z)\left|\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}d_{j,z}\right|\leq\widehat{\kappa}_{t-1}(z)

on the stated calibration event. An empirical inter-block mean difference is a diagnostic unless its relation to this predictable discrepancy has been validated.

Third term: nuisance error and score-level response transport.

For a given source round r=r⁡(j)r=r(j), write

pz​(a~∣c−)=gz,0​(a~∣c−),br​(a~∣c−)=gb,r​(a~∣c−),p_{z}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})=g_{z,0}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),\qquad b_{r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-})=g_{b,r}(\widetilde{a}\mid c^{-}),

and let

Δb,r,z​(a~,c−)=mb,r​(a~,c−)−mz​(a~,c−).\Delta_{b,r,z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})=m_{b,r}(\widetilde{a},c^{-})-m_{z}(\widetilde{a},c^{-}).

For the stored score in source round rr, write p^z,r=g^z,0,r\widehat{p}_{z,r}=\widehat{g}_{z,0,r} and m^z,r\widehat{m}_{z,r} for the fitted target joint law and response regression; the main text suppresses these fitting-cutoff indices. Let wz,r=pz/brw_{z,r}=p_{z}/b_{r} be the oracle joint ratio, w^z,r\widehat{w}_{z,r} the fitted clipped joint ratio, and w¯z,r=min⁡{wz,r,wmax}\bar{w}_{z,r}=\min\{w_{z,r},w_{\max}\} the clipped oracle ratio. Ratios are interpreted relative to a common dominating measure.

Under the exact nuisance decomposition in Appendix B.8, the third term has the following conditional algebra. Let νj=νzr⁡(j),ηr⁡(j)\nu_{j}=\nu_{z_{r(j)},\eta_{r(j)}}, pz=gz,0p_{z}=g_{z,0}, br⁡(j)=gb,r⁡(j)b_{r(j)}=g_{b,r(j)}, δm,j=m^z,r⁡(j)−mz\delta_{m,j}=\widehat{m}_{z,r(j)}-m_{z}, δw,j=w^z,r⁡(j)−w¯z,r⁡(j)\delta_{w,j}=\widehat{w}_{z,r(j)}-\bar{w}_{z,r(j)}, and Δb,r⁡(j),z=mb,r⁡(j)−mz\Delta_{b,r(j),z}=m_{b,r(j)}-m_{z}. With expectations taken under the source-window reference law and fitted quantities held fixed,

𝔼Pz,jeval​ψ^j,z−𝔼Pz,jeval​Vj,zlog​(C−)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}\widehat{\psi}_{j,z}-\mathbb{E}_{P_{z,j}^{\mathrm{eval}}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})
=\displaystyle={} 𝔼C−∼νj[∫𝒜~(p^z,r⁡(j)−pz)(a~∣C−)m^z,r⁡(j)(a~,C−)da~\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{j}}\Bigg[\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}(\widehat{p}_{z,r(j)}-p_{z})(\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\widehat{m}_{z,r(j)}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
+∫𝒜~(pz−br⁡(j)w¯z,r⁡(j))(a~∣C−)δm,j(a~,C−)da~\displaystyle\quad+\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}(p_{z}-b_{r(j)}\bar{w}_{z,r(j)})(\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\delta_{m,j}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
−∫𝒜~br⁡(j)(a~∣C−)δw,j(a~,C−)δm,j(a~,C−)da~\displaystyle\quad-\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}b_{r(j)}(\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\delta_{w,j}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\delta_{m,j}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}
+∫𝒜~[br⁡(j)w^z,r⁡(j)−pz](a~∣C−)Δb,r⁡(j),z(a~,C−)da~].\displaystyle\quad+\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\big[b_{r(j)}\widehat{w}_{z,r(j)}-p_{z}\big](\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\Delta_{b,r(j),z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}\Bigg]. (61)

For discrete joint treatments, the integrals are sums. The first three terms are bounded by the target-joint-law, clipping, and nuisance-product budgets. The last term is the score-level response-transport residual

ϵscore−resp,j​(z)=\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{score-resp},j}(z)={} 𝔼C−∼νj​|∫𝒜~[br⁡(j)​(a~∣C−)​w^z,r⁡(j)​(a~,C−)−pz​(a~∣C−)]​Δb,r⁡(j),z​(a~,C−)​𝑑a~|.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{j}}\left|\int_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}}\big[b_{r(j)}(\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\widehat{w}_{z,r(j)}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})-p_{z}(\widetilde{a}\mid C^{-})\big]\Delta_{b,r(j),z}(\widetilde{a},C^{-})\,d\widetilde{a}\right|. (62)

This term is distinct from the target-context response discrepancy ϵexp,r⁡(j)target​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r(j)}^{\mathrm{target}}(z) in Appendix B.9: the former is evaluated under the source context law and uses the fitted clipped ratio, whereas the latter is evaluated under the target context law and the target joint law. If |Δb,r,z|≤2​Bu|\Delta_{b,r,z}|\leq 2B_{u}, a conservative bound is

ϵscore−resp,j​(z)≤2​Bu​‖w^z,r⁡(j)−w¯z,r⁡(j)‖L1​(νj,br⁡(j))+ϵclip,j​(z),\epsilon_{\mathrm{score-resp},j}(z)\leq 2B_{u}\,\|\widehat{w}_{z,r(j)}-\bar{w}_{z,r(j)}\|_{L_{1}(\nu_{j},b_{r(j)})}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},j}(z), (63)

where

ϵclip,j(z)=2Bu𝔼C−∼νj𝔼A~∼br⁡(j)(⋅∣C−)[(wz,r⁡(j)−wmax)+].\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip},j}(z)=2B_{u}\,\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{j}}\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{A}\sim b_{r(j)}(\cdot\mid C^{-})}[(w_{z,r(j)}-w_{\max})_{+}].

This follows from pz−br⁡(j)​w¯z,r⁡(j)=br⁡(j)​(wz,r⁡(j)−wmax)+p_{z}-b_{r(j)}\bar{w}_{z,r(j)}=b_{r(j)}(w_{z,r(j)}-w_{\max})_{+} and does not assume that correcting the joint treatment law eliminates response transport.

Accordingly, the third term is bounded by the calibrated target-joint-law, clipping, and nuisance-product errors, plus ϵscore−resp,j​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{score-resp},j}(z) and any nuisance-distribution transfer allowance required to move the nuisance bounds to the reference evaluation law. The response discrepancy vanishes only under the relevant conditional response-invariance condition or an equivalent justified transport guarantee. Correcting the joint action/exposure distribution alone does not establish that condition.

Fourth term: context shift.

The fourth term compares expectations of the same source-response functional under the source context law and the target context law. It is controlled by the calibrated context-shift allowance in Appendix B.10. The calibration must apply to the relevant source round and historical averaging scheme; a context-distribution discrepancy without a justified function-class bound does not establish the required expectation bound.

Fifth term: target-law response transport.

The fifth term is controlled by the target-law exposure/response discrepancy in Appendix B.9. In particular,

|𝔼C−∼νz,0​Vj,zlog​(C−)−W∞​(z,0)|≤ϵexp,r⁡(j)target​(z)\left|\mathbb{E}_{C^{-}\sim\nu_{z,0}}V_{j,z}^{\mathrm{log}}(C^{-})-W_{\infty}(z;0)\right|\leq\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r(j)}^{\mathrm{target}}(z)

when the target value and source-response functional satisfy the definitions and identification conditions in that appendix.

The score-level discrepancy in Eq. (62) and the target-law discrepancy above are distinct contributions in this particular telescope. The single main-text budget ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) must be calibrated to dominate their historical average, as well as any exposure-representation error:

1Jt−1​∑j=1Jt−1[ϵscore−resp,j​(z)+ϵexp,r⁡(j)target​(z)].\frac{1}{J_{t-1}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t-1}}\left[\epsilon_{\mathrm{score-resp},j}(z)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp},r(j)}^{\mathrm{target}}(z)\right].

Alternatively, an independently justified tighter bound on the combined contribution may be used. If the existing ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) calibration controls only the target-law discrepancy, it must be extended to cover the score-level term as well. The component bounds are folded into the single ϵexp​(z)\epsilon_{\mathrm{exp}}(z) allowance; they are not then added again as separate response terms. The clipping allowance must also cover every clipping contribution actually retained in the exact nuisance decomposition. This is a clarification of the existing error budget, not a change to the main theorem’s core expression.

Combining the bounds.

Combining the stochastic fluctuation bound with the predictable-drift, nuisance, context-shift, and exposure/response-transport bounds yields the deviation inequality in Theorem 1, provided that the averaged non-statistical contributions are bounded by ϵ¯tot,t−1​(z)\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t-1}(z) and the predictable drift is bounded by κ^t−1​(z)\widehat{\kappa}_{t-1}(z) under the stated calibration.

The target-joint-law, clipping, and nuisance-product contributions must be calibrated for the actual source rounds and reference laws used in the estimator. The configuration-mismatch allowance is included only when needed to transfer nuisance guarantees across training and evaluation distributions; a response discrepancy already covered by the exposure/response budget must not be counted again. All component bounds must apply to the corresponding historical windows and their averaged contributions. A bound for a single evaluation round does not by itself bound the historical average.

A simultaneous guarantee over configurations requires a valid union or covering event, with the allocated failure probabilities included in the overall confidence budget. For a continuous configuration space, the covering argument must additionally account for an explicit Lipschitz covering remainder in the approximation/error budget; it does not follow from the union bound alone.

Empirical autocorrelation estimates and empirical inter-block mean differences are diagnostics only. They do not independently establish the required high-probability concentration, drift, identification, or transport events. The certificate therefore holds only when each component bound and the corresponding dependence and calibration conditions are justified.

D.4 Identification–Deployment Frontier: A Slow-Mixing Steady-State Hard Family

We construct a two-configuration, two-action, two-node steady-state family in which the parameter changes the no-exploration configuration value itself, normal deployment of either configuration is permitted, and the full adaptively collected log has information of order only 1+∑t=1Tηt1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}. The crucial mechanism is that ordinary deployment can repeatedly reveal the same latent state, whereas measurement exploration can refresh that state. This construction is valid as a horizon-indexed hard family when the model class does not impose a horizon-uniform bound on the mixing time. The latter qualification is mathematically essential and is discussed below.

Instance and steady-state target.

Fix a horizon T≥1T\geq 1 and a predetermined exploration schedule η1,…,ηT∈[0,1]\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{T}\in[0,1], and set ET=∑t=1TηtE_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}. Let θ∈{−1,+1}\theta\in\{-1,+1\} index the two environments, and define

qθ=12+θ​Δ,Δ=132​1+ET,εT=T−2.q_{\theta}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\theta\Delta,\qquad\Delta=\frac{1}{32\sqrt{1+E_{T}}},\qquad\varepsilon_{T}=T^{-2}.

There are two configurations 𝒵={z0,z1}\mathcal{Z}=\{z_{0},z_{1}\}, two actions 𝒜={a0,a1}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{0},a_{1}\}, and two network nodes sharing a latent state Ut∈{0,1}U_{t}\in\{0,1\}. The graph contains an edge between the nodes; the exposure of either node may be taken to be the realized action of its neighbor. This exposure and the static observed context are functions of the logged actions and do not reveal additional latent randomness. The latent state starts in its stationary law U0∼Ber⁡(qθ)U_{0}\sim\operatorname{Ber}(q_{\theta}). We take one post-burn-in observation window per slow round (T0=1T_{0}=1). Any prescribed fixed number of burn-in steps can be inserted as identity updates before this window: the controller is already in stationarity, and these steps reveal no extra observations. This is a legitimate (trivial) burn-in subcase of the black-box adaptation model.

Under either configuration, the no-exploration controller always chooses a0a_{0}. At slow round tt, each node independently selects a1a_{1} with probability ηt/2\eta_{t}/2 and a0a_{0} otherwise. Thus its action law is exactly

πz,ηtobs=(1−ηt)​δa0+ηt​ξ,ξ⁡(a0)=ξ⁡(a1)=12>0,\pi^{\mathrm{obs}}_{z,\eta_{t}}=(1-\eta_{t})\delta_{a_{0}}+\eta_{t}\xi,\qquad\xi(a_{0})=\xi(a_{1})=\tfrac{1}{2}>0,

independently of which configuration ztz_{t} was adaptively selected. Draw an unobserved spontaneous refresh marker Bt∼Ber⁡(εT)B_{t}\sim\operatorname{Ber}(\varepsilon_{T}) independently of all prior randomness. Define Jt=𝟏{Bt=1 or A1,t=a1 or A2,t=a1}J_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{B_{t}=1\text{ or }A_{1,t}=a_{1}\text{ or }A_{2,t}=a_{1}\}. If Jt=1J_{t}=1, refresh UtU_{t} as an independent Ber⁡(qθ)\operatorname{Ber}(q_{\theta}) draw; otherwise set Ut=Ut−1U_{t}=U_{t-1}. The observed normalized per-node reward is

Ri,t=gzt(Ut)−14𝟏{Ai,t=a1},gz0(u)=12,gz1(u)=u.R_{i,t}=g_{z_{t}}(U_{t})-\tfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{1}\{A_{i,t}=a_{1}\},\qquad g_{z_{0}}(u)=\tfrac{1}{2},\quad g_{z_{1}}(u)=u.

In particular, |Ri,t|≤1|R_{i,t}|\leq 1 and the observed logs contain the realized configuration, actions, graph/exposure context, and these rewards. The latent-state transition is not supplied to the operator. Each node’s exploratory action can refresh a shared state, and therefore affects future rewards of both nodes.

For any fixed configuration and fixed η\eta, the hidden-state chain is aperiodic and has the unique stationary distribution Ber⁡(qθ)\operatorname{Ber}(q_{\theta}), since a spontaneous refresh occurs with positive probability εT\varepsilon_{T}. A refresh draws from this same law, so the stationary distribution does not change with η\eta. Writing network utility as the average of the two node rewards, the no-exploration target values are exactly

W∞θ​(z0,0)=12,W∞θ​(z1,0)=12+θ​Δ.W^{\theta}_{\infty}(z_{0};0)=\tfrac{1}{2},\qquad W^{\theta}_{\infty}(z_{1};0)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\theta\Delta. (64)

The better configuration therefore depends on θ\theta, and the target value separation at z1z_{1} is 2​Δ2\Delta. This separation concerns the paper’s actual W∞​(z,0)W_{\infty}(z;0), not the reward of an action absent from the no-exploration target.

KL bound for every adaptive configuration-selection rule.

Let PθTP_{\theta}^{T} be the complete observed history under environment θ\theta, including any randomized configuration decisions. It suffices, by data processing, to upper-bound the KL of a more informative augmented experiment exposing U0U_{0} and every action, spontaneous refresh marker, and refreshed latent draw. Conditional on any augmented history, the algorithm’s configuration-selection kernel is the same function under the two environments, the action and spontaneous-marker kernels are identical, and only a newly sampled Ber⁡(qθ)\operatorname{Ber}(q_{\theta}) state contributes a likelihood difference. The chain rule hence gives

DKL(P+T∥P−T)≤d(Δ)(1+∑t=1T𝔼+[Jt]),d(Δ)=kl(Ber(12+Δ),Ber(12−Δ)).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{+}^{T}\|P_{-}^{T})\leq d(\Delta)\biggl(1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{+}[J_{t}]\biggr),\quad d(\Delta)=\mathrm{kl}\!\left(\operatorname{Ber}(\tfrac{1}{2}+\Delta),\operatorname{Ber}(\tfrac{1}{2}-\Delta)\right). (65)

Here

ℙ⁡(Jt=1)=1−(1−εT)​(1−ηt/2)2≤εT+ηt\mathbb{P}(J_{t}=1)=1-(1-\varepsilon_{T})(1-\eta_{t}/2)^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{T}+\eta_{t}

by the union bound. For 0<Δ≤1/320<\Delta\leq 1/32, d⁡(Δ)=2​Δ​log⁡1/2+Δ1/2−Δ≤16​Δ2d(\Delta)=2\Delta\log\frac{1/2+\Delta}{1/2-\Delta}\leq 16\Delta^{2}. Because T​εT=1/T≤1T\varepsilon_{T}=1/T\leq 1,

DKL(P+T∥P−T)≤16Δ2(2+ET)≤32Δ2(1+ET)≤132.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{+}^{T}\|P_{-}^{T})\leq 16\Delta^{2}(2+E_{T})\leq 32\Delta^{2}(1+E_{T})\leq\tfrac{1}{32}.

This upper bound accounts for all ordinary deployment observations, including repeated deployments of z1z_{1} with ηt=0\eta_{t}=0; they are potentially numerous but mostly repeat the same hidden Bernoulli state.

Value-identification lower bound.

By Pinsker’s inequality, TV⁡(P+T,P−T)≤(1/32)/2=1/8\operatorname{TV}(P_{+}^{T},P_{-}^{T})\leq\sqrt{(1/32)/2}=1/8. For any estimate W^\widehat{W} of W∞​(z1,0)W_{\infty}(z_{1};0), choose the sign corresponding to the closer target value in Eq. (64). A sign error forces |W^−W∞θ​(z1,0)|≥Δ|\widehat{W}-W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z_{1};0)|\geq\Delta. The two-point testing inequality therefore yields

infW^maxθ∈{−1,+1}⁡𝔼θ​|W^−W∞θ​(z1,0)|\displaystyle\inf_{\widehat{W}}\max_{\theta\in\{-1,+1\}}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}|\widehat{W}-W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z_{1};0)| ≥Δ2​(1−TV⁡(P+T,P−T))\displaystyle\geq\frac{\Delta}{2}\bigl(1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{+}^{T},P_{-}^{T})\bigr) (66)
≥7​Δ16≥1100​1+ET.\displaystyle\geq\frac{7\Delta}{16}\geq\frac{1}{100\sqrt{1+E_{T}}}. (67)

The infimum includes estimators using all logs and all adaptive configuration deployments. Thus the original cumulative-exploration rate holds for this horizon-indexed family.

Deployment loss on the same instance.

For every fixed configuration zz and exploration level η\eta, the stationary latent distribution is unchanged. Each node selects a1a_{1} with probability η/2\eta/2 and pays utility cost 1/41/4 on that action. Therefore

W∞θ​(z,0)−W∞θ​(z,η)=η/8.W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z;0)-W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z;\eta)=\eta/8.

For arbitrary adaptive configuration decisions and the fixed schedule,

DeploymentGapT=∑t=1T[W∞θ​(zt,0)−W∞θ​(zt,ηt)]=18​∑t=1Tηt.\mathrm{DeploymentGap}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl[W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z_{t};0)-W_{\infty}^{\theta}(z_{t};\eta_{t})\bigr]=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}. (68)

Consequently the two original-rate lower bounds hold simultaneously on one constructed family with universal constants c1=1/100c_{1}=1/100 and c2=1/8c_{2}=1/8.

Essential mixing-time qualification.

Under η=0\eta=0 the latent transition kernel is Kθ​(u,⋅)=(1−εT)​δu+εT​Ber⁡(qθ)K_{\theta}(u,\cdot)=(1-\varepsilon_{T})\delta_{u}+\varepsilon_{T}\operatorname{Ber}(q_{\theta}). It is geometrically mixing for every fixed horizon TT, with a decay factor (1−εT)k(1-\varepsilon_{T})^{k}, but its mixing time is of order T2T^{2}. The horizon-dependent mixing time is an explicit feature of the minimax class in Theorem 2: each fixed-TT process mixes geometrically, with mixing times of order T2T^{2} across the family. The bound therefore characterizes the stated predetermined exploration schedule and the associated horizon-dependent class. A horizon-uniform mixing restriction or an adaptively chosen measurement schedule defines a different lower-bound problem, with its own information budget and mixing assumptions.

D.5 CAUSAL-UCB Regret Proof

For each round t≥2t\geq 2, put W~t(z)=W^1:t−1(z;0)\widetilde{W}_{t}(z)=\widehat{W}_{1:t-1}(z;0) and let bt​(z)b_{t}(z) be the corresponding radius computed from the same past information, as specified in Algorithm 4.4. Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the simultaneously valid calibration/concentration event on which |W~t​(z)−W∞​(z,0)|≤bt​(z)|\widetilde{W}_{t}(z)-W_{\infty}(z;0)|\leq b_{t}(z) for every candidate and round. The event requires valid failure-probability allocation across rounds, configurations, and all calibration subevents in Appendix C.1.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, the optimism step zt∈arg⁡maxz​{W~t​(z)+bt​(z)}z_{t}\in\arg\max_{z}\{\widetilde{W}_{t}(z)+b_{t}(z)\} gives

W∞​(z⋆,0)\displaystyle W_{\infty}(z^{\star};0) ≤W~t​(z⋆)+bt​(z⋆)\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{W}_{t}(z^{\star})+b_{t}(z^{\star}) (69)
≤W~t​(zt)+bt​(zt),\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{W}_{t}(z_{t})+b_{t}(z_{t}), (70)

and therefore

W∞​(z⋆,0)−W∞​(zt,0)≤W~t​(zt)+bt​(zt)−W∞​(zt,0)≤2​bt​(zt).W_{\infty}(z^{\star};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)\leq\widetilde{W}_{t}(z_{t})+b_{t}(z_{t})-W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)\leq 2b_{t}(z_{t}).

For the first, uninitialized deployment t=1t=1, bounded rewards give a constant regret contribution (at most 2​Bu2B_{u}); the algorithm may use an arbitrary fixed tie-breaking rule when all initial radii are infinite. With

bt​(z)=2​Bψ​comp⁡(𝒵)+log⁡(2​T/δ)n¯eff,t−1​(z)+ϵ¯tot,t−1​(z)+κ^t−1​(z),b_{t}(z)=2B_{\psi}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})+\log(2T/\delta)}{\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z)}}+\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{tot},t-1}(z)+\widehat{\kappa}_{t-1}(z),

valid for t≥2t\geq 2, summing produces

RegT≤2​Bu+2​∑t=2Tbt​(zt).\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq 2B_{u}+2\sum_{t=2}^{T}b_{t}(z_{t}).

The simplification to the stated O~​(Bψ​T​comp⁡(𝒵))\widetilde{O}(B_{\psi}\sqrt{T\operatorname{comp}(\mathcal{Z})}) stochastic term requires the selected-arm, pre-deployment summability bound ∑t=2Tn¯eff,t−1(zt)−1/2=O~(T)\sum_{t=2}^{T}\underline{n}_{\mathrm{eff},t-1}(z_{t})^{-1/2}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}). It does not follow from optimism alone and need not hold under insufficient exploration. The additive deterministic terms then produce the conditional form in Theorem 3 (up to the harmless one-step index shift).

D.6 Deployment-Gap Corollary

If W∞​(z,η)W_{\infty}(z;\eta) is LWL_{W}-Lipschitz in η\eta uniformly over zz, then

W∞​(zt,0)−W∞​(zt,ηt)≤|W∞​(zt,0)−W∞​(zt,ηt)|≤LW​ηt.W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};\eta_{t})\leq|W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};\eta_{t})|\leq L_{W}\eta_{t}.

Summing gives

∑t=1T{W∞​(zt,0)−W∞​(zt,ηt)}≤LW​∑t=1Tηt.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\{W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};\eta_{t})\}\leq L_{W}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}.

This is separate from target regret: regret evaluates no-exploration configuration quality, while deployment gap evaluates the cost of collecting identifiable logs.

D.7 Proofs for the Restricted Local-Interference Certificate

This appendix proves Proposition 1 and Corollary 1. The claims are restricted to the specified homogeneous local-interference model; they do not assert that unknown target context laws or dependent black-box controllers can be certified from exploratory logs alone.

D.7.1 A simultaneous event for matched rewards

For each z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, expose the matched rewards in their order of observation, breaking ties within one network window by a fixed node order. Denote this sequence by Gz,1,Gz,2,…G_{z,1},G_{z,2},\ldots. The assumptions in the restricted model allow us to couple these observations to an independent, pre-generated sequence of draws distributed as clip⁡(μz+σ​Z,0,1)\operatorname{clip}(\mu_{z}+\sigma Z,0,1). Adaptive selection of zz only reveals a prefix of this sequence; the matched-reward distribution is unaffected by past configuration choices or by the indicator array.

The clipping map x↦clip⁡(x,0,1)x\mapsto\operatorname{clip}(x,0,1) is 11-Lipschitz. By Gaussian concentration, every matched reward is σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian around its mean WzW_{z} (the same statement holds when σ\sigma is a conservative sub-Gaussian scale bound). For every fixed m≥1m\geq 1,

Pr⁡(|1m​∑ℓ=1mGz,ℓ−Wz|>σ​2​Lm)≤2​e−L,L=log⁡2​K​(M+1)δ.\Pr\!\left(\left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}G_{z,\ell}-W_{z}\right|>\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2L}{m}}\right)\leq 2e^{-L},\qquad L=\log\frac{2K(M+1)}{\delta}. (71)

Here M=N​T​T0M=NTT_{0} is an upper bound on the total number of node-window reward slots in the entire experiment, and K=|𝒵|K=|\mathcal{Z}|. All means of observations in [0,1][0,1] differ by at most 11, so the radius may be truncated at 11. A union bound over the KK candidates and all nonempty prefix lengths 1≤m≤M1\leq m\leq M shows that the event

ℰmatch=⋂z∈𝒵⋂m=1M{|1m∑ℓ=1mGz,ℓ−Wz|≤ϵ(m)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{match}}=\bigcap_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\ \bigcap_{m=1}^{M}\left\{\left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}G_{z,\ell}-W_{z}\right|\leq\epsilon(m)\right\} (72)

has probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, because 2​K​M​e−L≤δ2KMe^{-L}\leq\delta. The event is defined on pre-generated streams and therefore also holds at all adaptively selected stopping and examination times. No sample splitting across examination times is required. At matched count m=0m=0, the prescribed predictor is 1/21/2, so |1/2−Wz|≤1/2=ϵ⁡(0)|1/2-W_{z}|\leq 1/2=\epsilon(0) deterministically.

Proof.

Fix any configuration zz and any nonempty prefix of nn network windows collected at its selected deployments. Put ej−=m^j−​(z)−Wze_{j-}=\widehat{m}_{j-}(z)-W_{z} and hj=Kj/(N​q)h_{j}=K_{j}/(Nq). For every scored window, an exact algebraic rearrangement gives

Yj,z−Wz\displaystyle Y_{j,z}-W_{z} =(1−hj)​ej−+1N​q​∑i=1NIj,i​(Rj,i−Wz).\displaystyle=(1-h_{j})e_{j-}+\frac{1}{Nq}\sum_{i=1}^{N}I_{j,i}(R_{j,i}-W_{z}). (73)

Summing over windows and taking absolute values yields

|W^z,n−Wz|\displaystyle|\widehat{W}_{z,n}-W_{z}| ≤1n​∑j=1n|1−hj|​|ej−|+mnn​N​q​|G¯z,mn−Wz|,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|1-h_{j}|\,|e_{j-}|+\frac{m_{n}}{nNq}\left|\overline{G}_{z,m_{n}}-W_{z}\right|, (74)

where the second term is interpreted as zero when mn=0m_{n}=0. Because the nuisance mean is computed from matched rewards strictly before the deployment round being scored, it is either the constant 1/21/2 or the mean of a prefix of length mj−m_{j-} of the same pre-generated matched-reward stream. On ℰmatch\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{match}}, for every scored window, simultaneously,

|ej−|≤ϵ⁡(mj−),|G¯z,mn−Wz|≤ϵ⁡(mn)when ​mn≥1.|e_{j-}|\leq\epsilon(m_{j-}),\qquad|\overline{G}_{z,m_{n}}-W_{z}|\leq\epsilon(m_{n})\quad\text{when }m_{n}\geq 1.

Substitution into (74) gives

|W^z,n−Wz|≤1n​∑j=1n|1−hj|​ϵ​(mj−)+mnn​N​q​ϵ​(mn)=bz,n.|\widehat{W}_{z,n}-W_{z}|\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|1-h_{j}|\epsilon(m_{j-})+\frac{m_{n}}{nNq}\epsilon(m_{n})=b_{z,n}.

Since Wz∈[0,1]W_{z}\in[0,1], Euclidean projection onto [0,1][0,1] cannot increase the distance to WzW_{z}, and therefore |W~z,n−Wz|≤bz,n|\widetilde{W}_{z,n}-W_{z}|\leq b_{z,n}. The reasoning holds for every zz and every prefix on the single event (72). For an unvisited configuration, |1/2−Wz|≤1/2|1/2-W_{z}|\leq 1/2 supplies the stated trivial interval. Finally, m^j−\widehat{m}_{j-}, KjK_{j}, mj−m_{j-}, mnm_{n}, qq, and ϵ⁡(⋅)\epsilon(\cdot) are functions only of past observed actions, matched rewards, and pre-specified constants. When used at decision round tt, the interval is computed from deployments completed strictly before round tt; it is thus a predecision certificate, not a post-hoc interval. ∎

D.7.3 Proof of Corollary 1

Proof.

Work on the simultaneous event of Proposition 1. Write cz,t−1=W~z,t−1c_{z,t-1}=\widetilde{W}_{z,t-1}, bz,t−1b_{z,t-1} for the radius available immediately before decision tt, and Uz,t−1=min⁡{1,cz,t−1+bz,t−1}U_{z,t-1}=\min\{1,c_{z,t-1}+b_{z,t-1}\}. The certificate and Wz∈[0,1]W_{z}\in[0,1] imply Uz,t−1≥WzU_{z,t-1}\geq W_{z} for every zz. Hence, for every noninitialization choice zt∈arg⁡maxz⁡Uz,t−1z_{t}\in\arg\max_{z}U_{z,t-1},

Wz⋆−Wzt\displaystyle W_{z^{\star}}-W_{z_{t}} ≤Uz⋆,t−1−Wzt≤Uzt,t−1−Wzt\displaystyle\leq U_{z^{\star},t-1}-W_{z_{t}}\leq U_{z_{t},t-1}-W_{z_{t}}
≤czt,t−1+bzt,t−1−Wzt≤2​bzt,t−1.\displaystyle\leq c_{z_{t},t-1}+b_{z_{t},t-1}-W_{z_{t}}\leq 2b_{z_{t},t-1}.

If upper bounds are used without clipping at 11, the same argument applies with Uz,t−1=cz,t−1+bz,t−1U_{z,t-1}=c_{z,t-1}+b_{z,t-1}. Every initialization round has regret at most 11 because Wz∈[0,1]W_{z}\in[0,1]. Adding at most HH such rounds proves

RegT≤H+2​∑t=H+1Tbzt,t−1.\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq H+2\sum_{t=H+1}^{T}b_{z_{t},t-1}.

∎

Scope of the result.

The confidence event above uses known qq, independent matched rewards, and a common target-law matched-reward mean. It does not require an independent target-context audit within this restricted model. In contrast, the general Theorem 1 requires separately valid target-action, context-transport, exposure, and dependence budgets. In particular, this restricted model does not establish matching optimal regret–inference or identification–deployment bounds for the general slow-mixing class of Theorem 2.

Appendix F Experimental Protocol, Data Provenance, and Metrics

F.1 Code and Evaluation Protocol

Exact source and commands.

The main controlled evaluation scripts are located in experiments/dependencies/certified_replication in the accompanying code archive. Install dependencies from requirements.txt, then execute the following commands from that directory:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python fast_compare.py --out results_final \
 --seeds 24 --T 200 --scenarios high_mismatch,low_mismatch
python audit_and_figures.py

The archive includes individual method–seed measurements, certified decision-round logs, seed-pairing metadata, protocol JSON, and a SHA-256 manifest. To reproduce the main tables and figures, run the commands above without modifying the declared protocol, reference files, or seed list.

Separation of three statistical objects.

For a deployed configuration ztz_{t}, target regret is computed with the oracle no-exploration target; deployment cost is the expected reward difference under the fixed exploration rate; uncertainty width is the worst-pair contrast diameter built from the valid predecision intervals. The evaluator never uses oracle values for nuisance fitting or selecting an action. The reported decision certificate uses the predecision radius throughout the evaluation.

Statistical setting.

The local-interference certificate uses known exposure neighborhoods, fixed exploration, independent matched rewards with specified noise scale, homogeneous targets, and untruncated weights. Its confidence guarantee is simultaneous over the finite evaluation horizon. Broader network models can be analyzed through the calibrated target-action, transport, and dependence budgets of Theorem 1. The trace-driven study uses its own semi-synthetic counterfactual construction, as described in Section 5.4.

F.2 Experimental Data Sources and Evaluation Scope

The controlled ring benchmark evaluates the predecision finite-sample certificate under known local interference. METR-LA and FlockLab supply trace-derived network structure and context observations, with model-generated counterfactuals and seed-level uncertainty. Each study is presented with its corresponding outcome and calibration model. Supplementary mechanism studies use separate sampling protocols and data sources; their results are reported separately from the primary benchmark.

Third-party data provenance.

The METR-LA input, metr-la.h5, is distributed through the DCRNN project  [32] (https://github.com/liyaguang/DCRNN). Our FlockLab input, 2019-07_FlockLab_sky.csv, comes from the July 2019 wireless-link traces associated with Jacob et al.  [33] (https://zenodo.org/records/3727526, Zenodo record v1.4.0).

Both sources are used only as network-derived context and topology inputs for offline semi-synthetic experiments; outcomes are model-generated. Neither the source files nor derived trace arrays are redistributed in the code supplement. Input filenames, archived hashes, and access links are documented in the supplement’s DATA_PROVENANCE.md.

F.3 Metric Definitions, Paired Comparisons, and Regret–Deployment Pareto Analysis

Metric inventory and interpretation.

The frozen controlled benchmark contains 336 method–seed records: two mismatch regimes, seven methods, and 24 paired seeds per regime. Each record includes cumulative target regret, terminal target-value gap, maximum pairwise ATE error, local audit width, and cumulative deployment gap. The field width_decision_certificate is populated as a decision-active radius only for Certified CAUSAL-UCB and Certified IPS-UCB. Widths for other methods are local diagnostic widths and do not imply simultaneous target coverage.

Paired-seed comparisons.

For a metric MM and a baseline bb, define the paired difference

Ds=MsCAUSAL​-​UCB−Msb.D_{s}=M_{s}^{\mathrm{CAUSAL\text{-}UCB}}-M_{s}^{b}.

For nn matched seeds, we report the mean difference and the paired Student-tt interval

D¯±t0.975,n−1​sDn,\bar{D}\ \pm\ t_{0.975,n-1}\frac{s_{D}}{\sqrt{n}},

where sDs_{D} is the sample standard deviation of the seed-level paired differences. A paired interval is not obtained by subtracting two marginal confidence intervals. Wilson intervals are used for binary full-path coverage outcomes. Zero-width empirical intervals in degenerate finite samples are not interpreted as zero population uncertainty.

Regret–deployment Pareto order.

We report cumulative target regret and cumulative expected deployment gap as separate objectives, both minimized. Method aa weakly dominates method bb on a given regime’s sample means if

Regreta≤Regretb,DeploymentGapa≤DeploymentGapb,\mathrm{Regret}_{a}\leq\mathrm{Regret}_{b},\qquad\mathrm{DeploymentGap}_{a}\leq\mathrm{DeploymentGap}_{b},

with at least one strict inequality for strict dominance. The empirical Pareto set contains methods not dominated by another method on these two sample means. This set is descriptive: mean non-dominance is not a significance test, and the expected deployment gap is calculated by the simulator rather than directly observed in a real deployment.

The high-mismatch sample-mean Pareto frontier is shown in main-text Figure 7(b); the low-mismatch counterpart is shown in Figure 9(c). These frontiers compare sample means and do not constitute significance tests.

Interpretation of the controlled comparison.

Under high mismatch, Certified CAUSAL-UCB, Certified IPS-UCB, and Greedy-Raw represent distinct non-dominated mean trade-offs: the certified DR method has the lowest regret but higher deployment cost, while Greedy-Raw has lower deployment cost but substantially higher regret. The reference methods with worse regret and higher deployment cost are dominated by at least one of these points in the reported means. Under low mismatch, the frontier is less discriminating because several methods trade small regret differences against small deployment-gap differences. The figure therefore complements the five-metric main table without ranking methods through an arbitrary weighted score.

Coverage and certificate width.

The audit-width column must be read with its provenance. For the two certified methods, the predecision radius enters the selection rule and has the stated finite-sample interpretation under the model conditions. For other methods, the recorded width is diagnostic only. Full-path certificate coverage is evaluated separately in Appendix H.1 and under hidden misspecification in Appendix H.2; these experiments use different protocols and are not pooled.

Appendix G Additional Experiments, Robustness, and Mechanism Studies

G.1 Robustness and Parameter Sweeps

Detailed robustness evidence.

The main table reports regret, terminal gap, causal-estimation error, audit width, and deployment gap as separate quantities. This appendix provides the full interference sensitivity panels and the complementary fixed-exploration and uncalibrated-drift stress diagnostics. The latter deliberately leave the validated drift regime and are interpreted as failure-boundary evidence, not theorem-certified coverage results.

Exploration-rate and deployment-cost diagnostics.

Figure 12 expands the measurement-cost comparison accompanying main-text Figure 7(a) and Figure 7(b). The exploratory logging rate is varied in a separate controlled sweep; deployment gap denotes measurement-induced utility loss and is distinct from target regret.

G.2 Trace-Driven Semi-Synthetic Comparisons

Protocol and comparison.

Figure 13 extends Table 3 by reporting cumulative target regret under both high- and low-mismatch regimes. The semi-synthetic replays use METR-LA and FlockLab topology/context traces with model-generated counterfactual outcomes, spanning 180 decision rounds and eight independent seeds per condition. The four panels separate dataset-specific effects from the influence of logging–target mismatch, while the 95% Student-tt intervals quantify seed-level variability.

Regime-dependent behavior.

Under high mismatch, CAUSAL-UCB achieves lower target regret than IPS-UCB on both METR-LA and FlockLab, consistent with the benefit of correcting exploratory measurements toward the deployment target. Under low mismatch, however, Greedy-Raw achieves lower regret on both traces, showing that the advantage of causal correction is not uniform across measurement regimes. These comparisons characterize empirical transfer and its limitations; they neither establish identification under arbitrary network interference nor extend the restricted ring-model certificate to trace-driven environments.

G.3 Seed-Level Outcomes and Sensitivity Summaries

The high-mismatch sample-mean Pareto frontier is shown in main-text Figure 7(b). Its low-mismatch counterpart is reported in Figure 9(c) in Appendix F.3; neither sample-mean frontier is a significance test. Only the two certified methods have a decision-active audit radius.

These known-local-exposure sensitivity studies use 24 independent paired seeds per setting and T=200T=200. The number and values of sweep levels are metric-specific and are shown in each panel; they are not forced to a common grid. Regret, ATE error, and deployment gap are summarized separately, with seed-level Student-tt intervals where shown.

Scope of context-shift and annealing diagnostics.

When the generator adds uncalibrated drift or changes η\eta over time, the fixed-exploration stationary proposition is inapplicable; measured coverage under these modifications is descriptive, not a valid extension of Theorem 1. These diagnostics are reported separately from the certified main benchmark and do not alter its theorem assumptions.

G.3.1 Auditable Contextual Support Extension

Figure 5 is a new, separate mechanism experiment, not an unchanged instance of the certified homogeneous ring generator. We preserve the fixed 24-node radius-one ring, the five-configuration setup, 24 seeds and paired target/logging sampling, but add context-dependent measurement flip probabilities and an explicit logging-induced context response. Let Xi=(X1​i,X2​i)X_{i}=(X_{1i},X_{2i}) denote the stationary pre-exploration latent context, generated from seeded, spatially smoothed Gaussian covariates. Conditional on XX, measurement flips are independent:

pi=η​σ​(0.95​X1​i−0.65​X2​i),Ai∼Ber⁡(pi),Ei=0.6​Ai+0.2​Ai−1+0.2​Ai+1.p_{i}=\eta\,\sigma(0.95X_{1i}-0.65X_{2i}),\qquad A_{i}\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_{i}),\qquad E_{i}=0.6A_{i}+0.2A_{i-1}+0.2A_{i+1}.

The unperturbed target has Ai=Ei=0A_{i}=E_{i}=0 and Ci0=XiC_{i}^{0}=X_{i}. Logging operates with

C1​iη=X1​i+0.90​Ei+0.16​η​X2,i−1,C2​iη=X2​i−0.62​Ei+0.26​η​X1,i+1.C_{1i}^{\eta}=X_{1i}+0.90E_{i}+0.16\eta X_{2,i-1},\quad C_{2i}^{\eta}=X_{2i}-0.62E_{i}+0.26\eta X_{1,i+1}.

Rewards are generated by clipping 0.62−0.60​Ei+0.075​C1​i−0.060​C2​i+ζi0.62-0.60E_{i}+0.075C_{1i}-0.060C_{2i}+\zeta_{i} to [0,1][0,1], with the same independent noise realization in target and logging simulator modes. The full-neighborhood conditional clean event probability is

qi(X)=∏j∈{i−1,i,i+1}(1−pj),Ii=𝟙{Ai−1=Ai=Ai+1=0}.q_{i}(X)=\prod_{j\in\{i-1,i,i+1\}}(1-p_{j}),\qquad I_{i}=\mathbb{1}\{A_{i-1}=A_{i}=A_{i+1}=0\}.

For each η∈{0.55,0.30,0.08}\eta\in\{0.55,0.30,0.08\} we sample 24 seeds, 20 spaced rounds and all 24 nodes, yielding 11,520 logging and 11,520 paired target records. The empirical clean rate is ∑Ii/n\sum I_{i}/n; the reported q10%q_{10\%} is the empirical tenth percentile of the true conditional qiq_{i}; the displayed IPW information index is (∑Ii/qi)2/(∑(Ii/qi)2)(\sum I_{i}/q_{i})^{2}/(\sum(I_{i}/q_{i})^{2}). This index is descriptive across dependent ring nodes, not the certified network-window effective sample size of Theorem 1. The paired target mode is available solely inside the simulator; no deployment algorithm observes its counterfactual data. Because these conditional propensities and context shifts violate assumptions of the previous certified fixed-η\eta submodel, no valid Theorem 1 certificate or regret conclusion is asserted for this extension. The figure is a mechanistic visualization of why context transport must be independently controlled even with positive conditional action support.

G.4 Matched-Log Mechanism Studies

Supplementary mechanism evidence comprises a 60-seed, 1,000-round factorial study and a matched-log DR-by-exposure study, alongside the primary controlled benchmark. Their sampling protocols and data sources are documented separately; results from distinct protocols are not pooled.

Study provenance.

The separate matched-log study reported DR/exposure ATE RMSE 0.03120.0312 and coverage 97.2%97.2\%, while its online comparison reported DR-UCB/local regret 18.96318.963 and CAUSAL-UCB regret 21.72321.723. That study used a distinct measurement design. The primary 24×20024\times 200 benchmark uses the controlled protocols and seed records described in Appendix F.1; the two sets of results are interpreted within their respective experimental settings.
