Information requirements and calibration cost.

The finite-state certificate combines independent observations of target context and action laws, target-regime response calibration, and a specified conditional mixing envelope. These quantities define the auditable black-box class in which the stated confidence event holds. Their measurement cost is included when interpreting the identification–deployment trade-off. The construction complements the local-interference certificate with a finite-state route to calibrating the general error decomposition.

G.5 Certified Optimism under Heterogeneous Initial Information

Question and controlled design.

We investigate when the confidence upper bounds constructed from the seven-term causal value certificate provide a useful configuration-level information acquisition mechanism, beyond the point estimates alone. The experiment uses the independently audited, finite-state black-box response model underlying our operational certificate test. There are three global configurations, two context states, and two possible local actions. In addition to logged rewards, external action/intervention and context audits are available; a known retained-block transition envelope controls dependence. These assumptions are sufficient for the audit construction, but are not implied by arbitrary black-box exploratory logs.

We compare Certified-OFU, selecting arg⁡maxz​{W^​(z,0)+bz}\arg\max_{z}\{\widehat{W}(z;0)+b_{z}\} (with target-value truncation), Certified-Greedy, selecting arg⁡maxz​W^​(z,0)\arg\max_{z}\widehat{W}(z;0), and a pre-specified decaying forced-exploration Greedy policy. All policies share identical nuisance fits, independent audits, initial scored windows, and configuration-specific potential score streams; only the choice rule differs. For a visited configuration, the certificate radius takes the form

bz​(n)=3.2​log⁡(2​K​Nmax/δs)2​n+∑j=17βz,j,δs=0.03,δaudit=0.02.b_{z}(n)=3.2\sqrt{\frac{\log(2KN_{\max}/\delta_{s})}{2n}}+\sum_{j=1}^{7}\beta_{z,j},\quad\delta_{s}=0.03,\ \delta_{\mathrm{audit}}=0.02. (86)

The seven nonnegative, independently audited buckets cover target action, nuisance product, clipping, exposure/response transport, context shift, cross-configuration transfer, and retained-block dependence/drift. The final bucket includes the explicit predictable-mean allowance 3.2​(0.45)63.2(0.45)^{6} for the known retained-block kernel Pz=λ​I+(1−λ)​𝟏​νz,log⊤P_{z}=\lambda I+(1-\lambda)\mathbf{1}\nu_{z,\mathrm{log}}^{\top}, λ=(0.45)6\lambda=(0.45)^{6}. The finite audit and martingale-score failure budgets sum to 0.050.05 for each independent run.

Initial-information regimes.

We fix five regimes before evaluating outcomes. The primary starved-optimal regime has target values (0.506,0.511,0.527)(0.506,0.511,0.527) and pilot scored-window allocations (1500,1500,120)(1500,1500,120); thus the truly optimal third configuration is initially least observed. Balanced-easy and balanced-ambiguous regimes use equal (900,900,900)(900,900,900) pilots; two further regimes assign the 120-window pilot to a suboptimal configuration instead. In each regime we evaluate 96 paired seeds, 80 online rounds, and 400 new scored retained blocks per round, with the same exploration mixture η=0.46\eta=0.46, independent 200,000200{,}000-sample audits per calibrated cell, and 10,00010{,}000 fitted observations per cell. Exact simulator target values are used only to assess regret and coverage, never by the learner.

Correction of an initial misranking.

In the starved-optimal regime, 33 of 96 independent seeds exhibit an initial point-estimate misranking. On these 33 paths, mean cumulative regret is 0.2320.232 for Certified-OFU and 1.0771.077 for Certified-Greedy; the paired mean difference (Greedy minus OFU) is 0.8450.845, with a seed-level descriptive 95% confidence interval [0.621,1.068][0.621,1.068]. The initial misranking persists in the point-estimate ordering for 22/33 Greedy paths at the final round. The full-sample difference across all 96 seeds remains positive, 0.2260.226 (95% CI [0.091,0.362][0.091,0.362]). These outcomes reveal a configuration-information bottleneck: a policy that never visits an underestimated candidate cannot shrink that candidate’s estimation uncertainty through selected-arm feedback.

The role of certificate tightness.

To test whether the advantage arises exclusively from the optimal configuration having a larger fixed seven-term budget, we repeat the starved-optimal regime after enlarging each of the seven arm-specific bias bounds to the maximum across all arms. This is still a valid, more conservative certificate and makes the fixed bias terms identical. On the 33 initial-misranking paths, equal-budget OFU obtains mean cumulative regret 0.7240.724 versus Greedy’s 1.0771.077; the paired difference is 0.3530.353 (95% CI [0.130,0.576][0.130,0.576]). Across all 96 paths, however, equal-budget OFU incurs 0.7240.724 regret versus Greedy’s 0.4670.467: conservative uncertainty induces unnecessary exploration when the point estimates are already adequate. The original arm-specific seven-term OFU achieves 0.2410.241 on these 96 paths, emphasizing the importance of certificate tightness as well as coverage validity.

Audit cost and interpretation.

All three policies spend 32,000 additional scored blocks per seed; independent intervention audits are a separate, substantial prerequisite. In the starved-optimal scenario, the model-based expected measurement-induced utility displacement ∑t[W∞​(zt,0)−W∞​(zt,η)]\sum_{t}[W_{\infty}(z_{t};0)-W_{\infty}(z_{t};\eta)] is approximately 3.3193.319 for Certified-OFU versus 3.1373.137 for Greedy (oracle-computed diagnostic, never used in selection). Thus improved target-regret control can coincide with greater measurement-induced utility displacement. The case study identifies when the OFU mechanism can correct point-estimation lock-in under valid audit assumptions; it does not imply OFU is uniformly optimal, nor does it extend the finite-state certificate automatically to unaudited networks. Tight certificates and meaningful information-growth conditions are both necessary ingredients when interpreting the regret result.

G.6 Gap–Noise–Budget Stress Test of Certified Optimism

To characterize when optimism helps and when it does not, we ran a predeclared 3×3×23\times 3\times 2 stress grid over target-value gap, response-noise level, and online scoring budget. The top-versus-middle target gap is Δ∈{0.005,0.016,0.030}\Delta\in\{0.005,0.016,0.030\}, the bounded-noise amplitude is σ∈{0.2,0.6,1.0}\sigma\in\{0.2,0.6,1.0\}, and the budget is 200 or 400 scored windows per decision. For response mean m⁡(c,a)m(c,a), the generated response is R=m⁡(c,a)+σ​min⁡{m⁡(c,a),1−m⁡(c,a)}​(2​U−1)R=m(c,a)+\sigma\min\{m(c,a),1-m(c,a)\}(2U-1) with U∼Unif⁡[0,1]U\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], preserving the conditional mean and the [0,1][0,1] bound. We use 24 paired seeds per cell, 80 online decisions, 10,000 fitting samples per cell, and 200,000 independent audit samples per cell. The paired comparison is Ds=RegretsOFU−RegretsGreedyD_{s}=\operatorname{Regret}_{s}^{\mathrm{OFU}}-\operatorname{Regret}_{s}^{\mathrm{Greedy}}; negative values favor OFU.

Across the 18 cells, OFU has lower mean regret in 12 cells and Greedy has lower mean regret in 6. The unweighted mean of the 18 cell-level paired differences is −0.0426-0.0426, but this average is descriptive because the cells represent different operating regimes. Only four cell-wise 95% paired-tt intervals lie entirely below zero, while two lie entirely above zero; the remaining intervals include zero. The results therefore support a conditional mechanism claim, not universal dominance by either policy.

Figure 26 summarizes the sensitivity patterns: OFU has lower mean regret in every smallest-gap cell, whereas Greedy performs better in the largest-gap, lowest-noise cells. The cell-wise values and paired intervals are given in Table 27 and Figure 27.

The seed count per cell is 24; it is a supplementary sensitivity analysis, while the 96-seed five-scenario experiment remains the primary mechanism study.

Appendix H Certificate Audits, Misspecification, and Failure Boundaries

H.1 Empirical Full-Path Validation of the Seven-Component Certificate

We evaluate the operational seven-component certificate under the finite-state, independently audited protocol specified in the finite-state audit construction in Appendix G.4.1. The experiment uses 300 independently seeded runs, 160 online rounds per run, and 2,000 scored windows per decision. Each run uses 10,000 frozen fitting observations and 200,000 independent observations per calibration cell. The seven-term attestation is constructed before online decisions; the simulator’s true target values are used only by the external evaluator and never by the policy.

A run is counted as covered only if every configuration’s target value lies inside its reported interval at every predecision time and at the terminal check. All 300 runs satisfy this full-path criterion (300/300; empirical rate 100%; Wilson 95% interval [0.9874,1.0000][0.9874,1.0000]). The OFU path inequality is also satisfied in all 300 runs. Mean cumulative regret is 1.0298 and the mean total seven-term bias budget is 0.0975 under this particular generator.

These results are an implementation-level check under the stated finite-state audit, target-intervention identification, and verified dependence-envelope assumptions. They are not a proof of 100% population coverage, and they do not establish that these assumptions can be inferred from exploratory logs alone. The additional audit observations are a substantive information cost and are not included in online regret.

H.2 Coverage under Hidden Calibration Misspecification

We directly stress the finite-state seven-term certificate by violating one assumption at a time while leaving the corresponding provenance flag falsely asserted as valid. Each condition contains 200 seeds, 120 online rounds per seed, 1,200 scored windows per decision, 1,000 fitting samples per cell, and 50,000 samples per cell claimed by the audit interface. The six hidden violations are: (i) the target action law differs from the audited target law; (ii) the target context distribution shifts after audit; (iii) the target interventional response shifts after audit; (iv) a context-dependent target–logging response transport effect is omitted; (v) the actual retained-block persistence is larger than the declared dependence envelope; and (vi) training estimates are reused as if they were independent audit estimates while the larger audit sample count is still claimed. The perturbation magnitudes are fixed as follows: for the third configuration, the target action probability for action 0 is reduced by 0.26 (with the complementary action probability adjusted accordingly); the target context law is changed to (0.88,0.12)(0.88,0.12); the target response is shifted upward by 0.17 and clipped to [0,1][0,1]; the transport stress shifts context-0 responses downward by 0.18 and context-1 responses upward by 0.18; the true persistence parameter is increased from the declared 0.450.45 to 0.920.92 with the same retained separation; and the audit-independence stress reuses 1,000 training estimates while falsely declaring 50,000 independent audit samples. The simulator’s true target values are used only for post-hoc coverage and regret evaluation.

The observed miss count is one out of 1,200 false certificate issuances, and it occurs in the target-response condition. This should not be interpreted as evidence that the certificate remains valid under misspecification: the theoretical guarantee does not apply when the stated assumptions are false. In this particular stress design, the reported intervals are wide (mean final average radius approximately 0.239–0.324), which often preserves empirical coverage despite invalid provenance. Thus the key failure is not necessarily immediate undercoverage; it is that the interface accepts a false attestation and cannot independently discover a concealed violation. The width result must be read alongside coverage rather than as a robustness guarantee.

As a control, we separately declared each corresponding required provenance flag invalid. The implementation rejected all six disclosed-invalid controls (6/6). This tests the software gate behavior only: it does not show that the gate can detect a false assertion that remains marked valid.

This experiment is a finite-simulation diagnostic, not a universal misspecification theorem. The severity and form of each perturbation are fixed as stated above; the observed coverage rates cannot be extrapolated to arbitrary violations. In particular, high empirical coverage under these perturbations is partly attributable to conservative, relatively wide intervals and does not validate the false assumptions.

H.2.1 Severity of concealed target-law misspecification

We further examine how the empirical validity of a previously issued seven-component certificate responds to the magnitude of an unreported target-law change. We retain the finite-state certificate interface and the same frozen training, independent audit, and logged-score streams across severity levels. Only the simulator’s target-regime law is changed without updating the attestation. For each of 64 paired seeds, the online algorithm evaluates three configurations for 120 rounds with 1,200 scoring windows per round. We prespecify magnitudes ξ∈{0,0.10,0.20,0.35,0.50}\xi\in\{0,0.10,0.20,0.35,0.50\} and test four target-law mechanisms: target-response means, target-action assignment probabilities, target-context mixture probabilities, and the action-specific target/logging response transport. The same online trajectory is tested against the resulting target value W∞ξ​(z,0)W^{\xi}_{\infty}(z;0), so the comparisons isolate a hidden identification failure rather than algorithmic random-seed changes.

At the largest target-response shift, none of the 64 paths remains covered, whereas the same certificate covers all paths with shifts at most 0.100.10. For exposure/transport shifts of magnitude 0.500.50, coverage is 15/6415/64. The target-context perturbation leaves the target value almost unchanged (maximum shift 0.00310.0031), and its high coverage must not be interpreted as robustness to a comparably large target-value error. The mean final certificate radius is 0.3260.326 and is unchanged across severity because it is computed from the unmodified attested evidence. The stress test therefore characterizes the failure boundary of an incorrectly attested certificate; it does not weaken the conditional coverage guarantee under correctly verified assumptions in Theorem 1.

Appendix I Limitations and Societal Implications

I.1 Limitations

Conditional validity of causal certificates.

The general value certificate depends on correctly specified and independently justified allowances for joint action–exposure overlap, target-law estimation, exposure and response transport, context shift, clipping, and temporal dependence. Observable discrepancy statistics and fitted effective sample sizes are diagnostics, not substitutes for validated bounds. If any required allowance cannot be calibrated, the resulting interval should not be interpreted as an operational coverage guarantee. The anytime finite-sample certificate in Proposition 1 applies only to its stated known-local-interference model; it does not certify the general black-box setting.

Scope and computational burden.

An incomplete exposure map can omit influential neighboring actions, and action-law correction alone cannot identify the no-exploration steady-state context distribution. Broad interference or weak joint overlap may therefore leave target values insufficiently identified. Evaluating multiple configurations also requires nuisance fitting, joint-exposure weighting, and calibration or auditing; these costs can increase with configuration count, exposure complexity, and dependence. We do not establish a general bound on wall-clock, memory, or audit cost for large production networks.

Limits of empirical generalization.

The controlled ring comparisons use 24 paired seeds over 200 rounds; the independent coverage audit is a separate protocol; and METR-LA/FlockLab experiments are 180-round semi-synthetic replays with eight seeds per condition and model-generated counterfactual outcomes. They are not live deployment tests or evidence that the general certificate is calibrated on either trace. Under low mismatch, Greedy-Raw can outperform CAUSAL-UCB in target regret; under high mismatch, lower target regret can come with greater measurement-induced deployment loss. Hence neither uniform superiority nor deployment safety follows from these experiments.

I.2 Potential Societal Impacts and Responsible Deployment

Correcting the discrepancy between logged exploratory rewards and no-exploration target values could improve the auditability of network-wide configuration choices and make measurement costs more visible. However, in operational networks, exploration itself may degrade service, and optimizing an aggregate utility can conceal disproportionate effects on individual nodes, users, or regions. Misspecified exposure representations or unverified transport assumptions could also produce overconfident decisions. Depending on the application, fine-grained network telemetry may create privacy or security risks.

Before any real-world use, system operators should assess application-specific safety constraints, impose exploration budgets and fallback or rollback rules, examine disaggregated service-quality outcomes, minimize access to sensitive telemetry, and independently validate the certificate’s required assumptions and error allowances. These are proposed deployment precautions, not safeguards experimentally implemented or certified in the present study.
